Abstract

Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider–mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.

1 Introduction

Missing data are common in social science research. Through a review of published observational causal studies in the American Journal of Political Science (AJPS) and American Political Science Review (APSR) between 2019 and 2024, Huang and Liu (2026) found that more than 50% of the studies mentioned missing values. Our review of a reconstructed sample of theirs finds that 80 of 158 articles (50.6%) state or imply listwise deletion in the main text, compared with 42 (26.6%) reporting any fill-in method and 11 (7.0%) describing an imputation model. Further, listwise deletion could also arise from software defaults: in R, lm(), glm(), and ivreg() drop incomplete observations under default na.action = na.omit, and mediation analyses may inherit these sample restrictions from their component models44 4 mediate() refits mediator and outcome models on their overlapping observations when dropobs = TRUE (Tingley et al. 2014)..

Multiple imputation uses partially observed records and can reduce bias and improve precision (King et al. 2001; Honaker and King 2010; Lall 2016), but under nonignorable missingness it can perform worse than listwise deletion (Pepinsky 2018). Listwise deletion avoids an imputation model and can yield consistent coefficient estimates under some nonrandom missingness (Arel-Bundock and Pelc 2018), yet it discards observed information and can introduce selection bias (Heckman 1979; King et al. 2001; Huang and Liu 2026).

In this paper, we study when regression after listwise deletion can be justified. Among the 80 articles that state or imply listwise deletion, 45 (56%) report at least one regression estimated after dropping cases with missing values55 5 These counts are lower bounds. Appendix A details the sample construction and coding rules.. Thus, we consider the following causal-regression workflow for listwise deletion: a researcher chooses an adjustment set intended to identify the population average treatment effect (ATE) and a regression specification intended to estimate it as if all required values were observed, then applies listwise deletion and reports the treatment coefficient from the complete-case regression as an estimate of that ATE. We develop a formal framework for this decision by making the assumed causes of missingness explicit and deriving conditions under which the complete-case regression consistently estimates the researcher’s target.

Taking the oracle regression’s identification of a variance-weighted average treatment effect as given, we formalize sufficient conditions under which regression after deletion consistently estimates the population ATE. Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, researchers must check two boxes: whether treatment comparisons remain valid after selection into the complete-case sample, and whether the fitted regression pools those comparisons appropriately. The first asks researchers to add the missing indicator and its causes to the DAG used to justify their original adjustment set, then reassess adjustment and treatment overlap. The second asks whether the outcome specification remains correct among complete cases, or whether treatment-propensity weighting can instead recover their average effect. With heterogeneous effects, a third box connects complete-case comparisons to the population target: when conditional effects are transportable to the population, researchers need to average them over the population covariate distribution rather than the complete-case covariate distribution. These checks provide a formal framework for assessing the causal and modeling assumptions behind complete-case regression, which require substantive judgment beyond statistical tests: as Subsection 4.2 illustrates, the same observed data can imply different conclusions about the validity of listwise deletion under different causal structures.

We also show why each box requires a separate check. In one simulation, selection leaves within-covariate treatment comparisons valid but changes the outcome specification, causing complete-case regression to pool those comparisons incorrectly. In the collider–mediator illustration, the same missing mechanism and MAR classification call for different adjustment choices depending on whether a covariate is a mediator or a confounder. Finally, the reweighting applications show how valid complete-case effects can differ from the population ATE when treatment effects vary and the covariate distributions differ.

Our approach builds on graphical analyses of selection bias and missing data. Bareinboim and Pearl (2012), Bareinboim, Tian and Pearl (2014), and Bareinboim and Pearl (2016) study when statistical and causal quantities can be recovered from selected data. Mohan and Pearl (2021) develop the corresponding missing-data perspective. Daniel et al. (2012) and Saadati and Tian (2020) establish graphical conditions for causal analysis using complete records. Ross, Breskin and Westreich (2020) show how effect modification and differences in covariate distributions affect marginal complete-case estimates. Hughes et al. (2019), most closely related, use causal diagrams to illustrate when complete-case regression yields unbiased estimates, taking the validity of the full-data analysis as given, but do not provide formal proofs. Building on their perspective, we derive and prove sufficient conditions that distinguish valid treatment comparisons among complete cases, which graphical criteria address, from the regression’s pooling of those comparisons, which they alone do not guarantee. Together, these results bring graphical criteria for listwise deletion into the regression workflow used by applied political scientists, who, to our knowledge, do not currently use causal diagrams to justify deletion. Our framework thus gives applied researchers a practical set of checks for assessing whether their complete-case regression consistently estimates the ATE of interest.

Our framework also reconciles the differing recommendations of Pepinsky (2018) and Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018) by specifying the causal and modeling assumptions under which they apply, complements guidance on choosing imputation models (Marbach 2022) by clarifying when deletion is justified in the first place, and generalizes the identification conditions underlying Huang and Liu (2026): we clarify when their imputation step is needed to recover the population covariate distribution and when complete-case effects can instead be averaged using an observed population distribution.

In Section 2, we use a simulation to build intuition for the two sufficient conditions: with a constant unit-level treatment effect, we contrast three missing-not-at-random mechanisms under which complete-case regression respectively recovers the population ATE, requires a pooling remedy, and fails because within-covariate comparisons are invalid.

Section 3 then derives formal sufficient conditions under which complete-case regression consistently estimates the population ATE: when within-strata treatment comparisons among complete cases identify causal effects, when regression pools them appropriately, and how the resulting effect connects to the population ATE under constant or heterogeneous effects.

Section 4 revisits conventional guidance, recovering familiar recommendations as special cases and showing how a covariate’s role as mediator or confounder changes the validity of listwise deletion under the same missingness pattern and MAR classification.

Section 5 develops reweighting for heterogeneous effects, generalizing the identification argument underlying Huang and Liu’s (2026) two-stage projection estimator, and then illustrates it in a reanalysis of Bodea and Hicks (2015). Appendix F shows the potential of extension into generalized linear models.

Section 6 brings all three checks together in a reanalysis of the canvassing experiment (Kalla and Broockman 2023), illustrating the application of the three box roadmap we propose.

2 Motivating Simulation: Identification and Weighting

We begin with a simulation to illustrate conditions under which complete-case regression consistently estimates the population ATE, the causal effect that the oracle adjustment set identifies. The oracle sample contains Nor=20,000N_{\mathrm{or}}=20{,}000 observations generated by the following process, with a constant unit-level treatment effect τ=1\tau=1:

Yi=Di+Xi+Ui+ξi,ξi∼N⁡(0,0.52).Y_{i}=D_{i}+X_{i}+U_{i}+\xi_{i},\qquad\xi_{i}\sim N(0,0.5^{2}).

The pretreatment confounder XiX_{i} is uniform on {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, while the unobserved cause of the outcome, UiU_{i}, is also uniform on {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. XiX_{i}, UiU_{i}, and ξi\xi_{i} are mutually independent. Treatment assignment depends only on XiX_{i}: Di|Xi=x∼Bernoulli⁡((1+x2)/4+0.30​x)D_{i}\mid X_{i}=x\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}((1+x^{2})/4+0.30x).

In the observed data, YiY_{i} and DiD_{i} are available for all 20,000 observations, but XiX_{i} is missing for some. Let Mi=0M_{i}=0 when XiX_{i} is observed and Mi=1M_{i}=1 otherwise. We consider three mechanisms governing whether XiX_{i} is observed:

A:P(Mi=0∣Xi=x,Ui=u)\displaystyle\text{A:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid X_{i}=x,U_{i}=u) =0.95−0.30​x2,\displaystyle=0.95-0.30x^{2},
B:P(Mi=0∣Xi=x,Ui=u)\displaystyle\text{B:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid X_{i}=x,U_{i}=u) =(0.95−0.30​x2)​(1+0.50​u​x2),\displaystyle=(0.95-0.30x^{2})(1+0.50ux^{2}),
C:P(Mi=0∣Xi=x,Ui=u,Di=d)\displaystyle\text{C:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid X_{i}=x,U_{i}=u,D_{i}=d) =(0.95−0.30​x2)​[1+0.50​u​(2​d−1)​x2].\displaystyle=(0.95-0.30x^{2})[1+0.50u(2d-1)x^{2}].

All three mechanisms are not missing at random (NMAR): whether XiX_{i} is observed depends on its unobserved value. Under B, observation further depends on UiU_{i}, while under C, it additionally depends on the interaction between UiU_{i} and DiD_{i}. Averaging over UiU_{i}, each mechanism gives P⁡(Mi=0∣Xi=x)=0.95−0.30​x2P(M_{i}=0\mid X_{i}=x)=0.95-0.30x^{2}. Because XiX_{i} is uniform on {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, the missingness rate is P⁡(Mi=1)=0.25P(M_{i}=1)=0.25 in all three cases.

An analyst could use listwise deletion to fit the following linear regression among complete cases:

Yi=αcc+βcc​Di+γcc​Xi+εsim,i,Mi=0.Y_{i}=\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}+\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}D_{i}+\gamma_{\mathrm{cc}}X_{i}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sim},i},\qquad M_{i}=0.

One rationale for this choice is the advice66 6 An analyst might read Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018) as endorsing listwise deletion here, because the oracle error Ui+ξiU_{i}+\xi_{i} is independent of XiX_{i} and DiD_{i} and missingness depends only on XiX_{i}. But their advice also requires the complete-case indicator to be independent of the regression error—exactly what mechanisms B and C violate, since MiM_{i} is associated with Ui+ξiU_{i}+\xi_{i} given XiX_{i} and DiD_{i}. Their advice therefore excludes these cases. of Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018, p. 243):

Under [the pattern of missingness driven by values of the independent variables], LWD can be used without fear that it will introduce bias in regression estimates.

Alternatively, an analyst might use multiple imputation to fit the same regression, guided by the general expectation expressed by King et al. (2001, p. 51):

Thus, multiple imputation will normally be better than, and almost always not worse than, listwise deletion.

We examine how both choices perform under each mechanism, benchmarking against the oracle estimator and adding a complete-case estimator that uses inverse treatment-propensity weights (CC + IPW) (Choi, Dekkers and le Cessie 2019). Figure 1 summarizes the treatment-coefficient estimates across 500 replications:

Under mechanism A, the unweighted complete-case estimates are centered on τ=1\tau=1, consistent with Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018)’s result that listwise deletion need not bias regression estimates when missingness depends on regressor values. The multiple-imputation estimates instead average 1.057: being NMAR in mechanism A, the consistency guarantee for correctly specified imputation under MAR does not apply. Under mechanism B, both the unweighted complete-case and multiple-imputation estimates are centered above τ=1\tau=1. For complete-case regression, MiM_{i} depends on both XiX_{i} and UiU_{i} and is therefore associated with the oracle regression error Ui+ξiU_{i}+\xi_{i}, violating the indicator–error independence condition of Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018). The CC + IPW estimates remain centered near one. Under mechanism C, none of the three feasible estimators produces estimates centered on τ=1\tau=1.

Sources of Error

These patterns reflect two sources of error: treatment comparisons within XiX_{i} strata may fail to identify τ\tau, or the pooled regression may fail to preserve valid within-stratum comparisons in its treatment coefficient. Table 1 reports the mean estimated intercepts and treatment coefficients from separate complete-case regressions of YiY_{i} on DiD_{i} in each XiX_{i} stratum.

Weighting

To examine pooling, we first allow the intercept and treatment coefficient to vary across values of XiX_{i}:

Yi=αXi+βXiDi+εstr,i,Mi=0,E[εstr,i∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=0.Y_{i}=\alpha_{X_{i}}+\beta_{X_{i}}D_{i}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{str},i},\qquad M_{i}=0,\qquad E[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{str},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=0.

Among complete cases with Xi=xX_{i}=x, untreated units have mean outcome αx\alpha_{x}, and treated units have mean outcome αx+βx\alpha_{x}+\beta_{x}. Thus, βx\beta_{x} is their observed difference in means. Whether this difference identifies the causal effect τ\tau depends on the missing mechanism. The residual εstr,i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{str},i} captures individual deviations from these group means.

Under mechanisms A and B, β−1=β0=β1=τ=1\beta_{-1}=\beta_{0}=\beta_{1}=\tau=1, as reflected in Table 1. The baseline means αx\alpha_{x} differ: (α−1,α0,α1)=(−1,0,1)(\alpha_{-1},\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1})=(-1,0,1) under A and (−0.5,0,1.5)(-0.5,0,1.5) under B. A linear XiX_{i} term captures αx\alpha_{x} under A but not under B. Thus, the pooled complete-case regression on DiD_{i} and linear XiX_{i} consistently estimates τ\tau under A but not under B, due to the misspecification of the control variables XiX_{i} under B.

Under mechanism B, selection into complete cases depends on UiU_{i}: at Xi=±1X_{i}=\pm 1, units with Ui=1U_{i}=1 are more likely to be complete than units with Ui=−1U_{i}=-1. The oracle regression error therefore has a nonzero conditional mean among complete cases, 𝔼[Ui+ξi∣Xi,Di,Mi=0]=Xi2/2\mathbb{E}[U_{i}+\xi_{i}\mid X_{i},D_{i},M_{i}=0]=X_{i}^{2}/2. Since Yi​(0)=Xi+Ui+ξiY_{i}(0)=X_{i}+U_{i}+\xi_{i}, the mean untreated outcome becomes 𝔼[Yi(0)∣Xi,Mi=0]=Xi+Xi2/2\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(0)\mid X_{i},M_{i}=0]=X_{i}+X_{i}^{2}/2, the added Xi2/2X_{i}^{2}/2 cannot be represented by the intercept and linear XiX_{i} term in the fitted regression. Thus, correct oracle specification, linear XiX_{i}, does not ensure correct specification among complete cases.

Alternatively, IPW can estimate causal effects without specifying how XiX_{i} enters the outcome regression (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983; Hirano, Imbens and Ridder 2003). Under mechanism B, the IPW estimator in Figure 1 weights each complete case by the inverse probability of its observed treatment given XiX_{i} and Mi=0M_{i}=0. Its estimates are centered near the complete-case ATE, which equals the constant population ATE77 7 Appendix B.1 explains how IPW and saturated regression weight the within-XX comparisons differently under mechanisms B and C..

Back-door adjustment criterion

We next compare mechanisms B and C. In Figure 1, the IPW complete-case estimates are centered near τ=1\tau=1 under B but not C, although treatment probabilities are correctly specified within each XiX_{i} stratum under both mechanisms. The difference is that βx=τ=1\beta_{x}=\tau=1 in every XiX_{i} stratum under B, whereas β−1\beta_{-1} and β1\beta_{1} do not identify τ\tau under C.

To assess why the within-stratum comparisons differ, we use Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) from Pearl (1995), including the missingness indicator MiM_{i} as a node, to trace the paths that conditioning on complete-case status opens. Figure 2 presents the DAGs for mechanisms B and C.

Under B, conditioning on the collider MiM_{i} opens the noncausal path Di←Xi→Mi←Ui→YiD_{i}\leftarrow X_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow U_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, but conditioning on XiX_{i} blocks it. Thus, {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion, yielding Yi​(d)⟂Di|Xi,MiY_{i}(d)\perp D_{i}\mid X_{i},M_{i} for d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}—the within-complete-case exchangeability condition emphasized by Choi, Dekkers and le Cessie (2020). The within-XiX_{i} treatment contrast among complete cases therefore identifies τ=1\tau=1.

Under C, conditioning on Mi=0M_{i}=0 opens the noncausal path Di→Mi←Ui→YiD_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow U_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, which conditioning on XiX_{i} does not block. Thus, {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} fails the adjustment criterion’s path-blocking requirement. In this simulation, the within-XiX_{i} treatment contrasts at Xi=−1X_{i}=-1 and Xi=1X_{i}=1 do not identify τ\tau.

To sum up, all three mechanisms are NMAR and, by construction, share the same probability of missingness conditional on XiX_{i}, yet they differ in whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the population ATE, for two reasons. Under A, the within-XiX_{i} comparisons identify τ\tau and the pooled linear regression recovers it. Under B, the comparisons still identify τ\tau, and entering XiX_{i} categorically or using treatment IPW restores consistent estimation. Under C, the comparisons fail to identify τ\tau in two strata, and neither approach recovers it. These differences motivate the formal results in Section 3, which establish sufficient causal and modeling conditions for complete case regressions to consistently estimate the population ATE.

3 Identification of Population ATE under Complete-Case Regression

In this section, we first prove that two conditions are sufficient for complete-case regression to consistently estimate the complete-case average treatment effect: (a) treatment comparisons within covariate strata identify the stratum-specific causal effects, and (b) the fitted estimator aggregates those comparisons correctly. Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, the complete-case ATE equals the population ATE. With heterogeneous effects, recovering the population ATE requires a third condition: the conditional effects identified among complete cases must also transport to the population, and complete cases must cover the population covariate support. These effects can then be averaged over the population covariate distribution.

Our proof develops in four parts. First, we define the oracle regression benchmark and distinguish missing patterns from missing mechanisms. Second, we use a DAG with a missing indicator to assess within-covariate treatment comparisons among complete cases. Third, we examine when outcome specification or treatment-propensity weighting allows regression to aggregate those comparisons correctly. Finally, we connect the complete-case ATE to the population ATE. Section 5 develops reweighting under heterogeneous effects.

3.1 Oracle Regression and Missingness

We first distinguish the missing mechanism from the missing pattern. A missing pattern describes which variables are missing for a unit. A missing mechanism specifies how the probability of that pattern depends on the full-data values (Little and Rubin 2019). Missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and not missing at random (NMAR) classify missing mechanisms88 8 Under MCAR, missingness probabilities are independent of data values. Under MAR, missingness may depend on variables whose values are observed, but not on the values that are missing under that pattern. NMAR permits dependence on those missing values.. While frequently used, these classifications usually do not specify which variables are missing or, more importantly for our framework, what causes the missingness.

Missing Pattern and Missing Mechanism

In our motivating simulation, mechanisms A, B, and C are all NMAR and share the same missing pattern: XiX_{i} is missing for some units. They differ, however, in how observation of XiX_{i} depends on XiX_{i}, UiU_{i}, and DiD_{i}. These differences determine whether complete-case regression consistently estimates τ\tau and, if not, whether saturation or treatment IPW can help. The NMAR label alone therefore does not distinguish the assumptions that matter for these estimators99 9 The importance of specifying the missing mechanism precisely has also been raised by Seaman et al. (2013), who distinguish different formal definitions of MAR..

Formally, for a unit ii, let Xi=(Xi1,…,Xip)X_{i}=(X_{i}^{1},\ldots,X_{i}^{p}) collect the pretreatment covariates in the researcher’s chosen adjustment set1010 10 Throughout, we take the chosen adjustment set to include any pretreatment treatment-effect moderators used in the analysis., and let Vi=(Yi,Di,Xi1,…,Xip)V_{i}=(Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i}^{1},\ldots,X_{i}^{p}) additionally contain the treatment indicator DiD_{i} and the outcome YiY_{i}.

Definition 1 (Missing pattern and omnibus missing indicator).

For unit ii, let MiYM_{i}^{Y}, MiDM_{i}^{D}, and MiXjM_{i}^{X^{j}}, for j=1,…,pj=1,\ldots,p, equal one when the corresponding value of YiY_{i}, DiD_{i}, or XijX_{i}^{j} is missing, and zero otherwise. The vector

𝐌i=(MiY,MiD,MiX1,…,MiXp)\mathbf{M}_{i}=(M_{i}^{Y},M_{i}^{D},M_{i}^{X^{1}},\ldots,M_{i}^{X^{p}})

is unit ii’s missing pattern. Complete-case regression uses only units for which every component of ViV_{i} is observed. To represent this restriction, we summarize the missing pattern with an omnibus indicator. Define

Mi={MiY+MiD+∑v=1pMiXv>0}.M_{i}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{M_{i}^{Y}+M_{i}^{D}+\sum_{v=1}^{p}M_{i}^{X^{v}}>0\right\}.

Thus Mi=0M_{i}=0 if and only if YiY_{i}, DiD_{i}, and every component of XiX_{i} are observed1111 11 The omnibus missing indicator corresponds to Wooldridge’s (2002, p. 553) selection indicator with reversed coding: Mi=1−siM_{i}=1-s_{i}. Both indicators are defined for all units in the underlying population, including those excluded from estimation. They can therefore represent listwise deletion due to missing values in the outcome, regressors, or both..

If a researcher changes the adjustment set, the missing indicator and complete-case sample may also change, so the researcher must redefine the indicator and reassess the conditions for the revised specification.

Appendix D.2 provides the conventional probabilistic definition of a missing mechanism (Little and Rubin 2019; Seaman et al. 2013). In the next subsection, we give the mechanism a causal formulation, building on graphical models of missing data (Mohan and Pearl 2021).

Our analysis from now on focuses on the missing mechanism: what causes a unit to enter the complete-case sample and how that selection affects treatment effect identification and estimation. We represent selection into this sample using the omnibus missing indicator MiM_{i}, regardless of which variable makes a unit incomplete.

Oracle Samples

To assess how selection into complete cases affects the regression workflow, we first define its benchmark before listwise deletion: the oracle sample, in which all required values are observed and for which the researcher chooses an adjustment set and regression specification. We distinguish two versions of these sampled units to connect the regression benchmark to the causal effect of interest.

The oracle potential-outcome sample contains both potential outcomes and lets us define the causal effect. The oracle sample contains each unit’s realized outcome, treatment, and required covariates, including values missing in the observed data. We call the chosen regression applied to the oracle sample the oracle regression and ask whether fitting the same specification to complete cases recovers the population ATE that this adjustment set identifies.

We maintain Assumption A1 (SUTVA) to link potential outcomes to each unit’s realized outcome, and denote the population distribution from which the oracle potential-outcome sample is drawn by PpoP_{\mathrm{po}}. The assumption and formal definitions of both oracle samples are in Appendix D.

Oracle Regression

The target causal estimand is the population average treatment effect:

τ≡𝔼Ppo​[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)].\tau\equiv\mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathrm{po}}}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)].

We take the researcher’s chosen oracle regression as our benchmark:

Yi=βor​Di+b​(Xi)⊤​γor+εor,i.Y_{i}=\beta_{\mathrm{or}}D_{i}+b(X_{i})^{\top}\gamma_{\mathrm{or}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}. (1)

Here b⁡(Xi)b(X_{i}) contains an intercept and the chosen covariate terms. βor\beta_{\mathrm{or}} and γor\gamma_{\mathrm{or}} are the population treatment and covariate coefficients, and εor,i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i} is the residual. Their sample estimates are β^or\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{or}} and γ^or\widehat{\gamma}_{\mathrm{or}}.

We assume that the researcher’s causal identification assumptions make XiX_{i} a valid adjustment set, so that the population ATE would be identified if all required values were observed. Even with a valid adjustment set, however, the oracle regression coefficient βor\beta_{\mathrm{or}} may not equal the population ATE. It equals τ\tau under a constant treatment effect with correctly specified covariate terms, or under a constant treatment propensity, as in a randomized experiment. With heterogeneous effects, it is instead a variance-weighted average of conditional effects (Angrist and Pischke 2009; Aronow and Samii 2016). We therefore target τ\tau directly without requiring βor=τ\beta_{\mathrm{or}}=\tau. Under standard OLS regularity conditions, the sample coefficient β^or\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{or}} converges in probability to βor\beta_{\mathrm{or}}. Although we focus on the population ATE, some results also apply to other causal estimands targeted by the oracle regression, as discussed after Proposition 3.

After listwise deletion, the researcher fits the same specification to complete cases:

Yi=βcc​Di+b​(Xi)⊤​γcc+εcc,i,Mi=0.Y_{i}=\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}D_{i}+b(X_{i})^{\top}\gamma_{\mathrm{cc}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i},\qquad M_{i}=0. (2)

Here βcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}} and γcc\gamma_{\mathrm{cc}} are the population regression coefficients among complete cases, and εcc,i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i} is the corresponding residual. Under standard OLS regularity conditions, the sample treatment coefficient β^cc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}} converges in probability to βcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

To summarize the problem, our question is whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the population ATE identified by the oracle regression’s adjustment set. When βor=τ\beta_{\mathrm{or}}=\tau, this requires

βcc=βor.\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\beta_{\mathrm{or}}.

When βor\beta_{\mathrm{or}} differs from τ\tau, equality between the two regression coefficients would no longer be sufficient to recover the population ATE. In either case, we take the oracle adjustment set’s validity as given and focus on the additional causal and modeling conditions needed for regression after listwise deletion to recover τ\tau.

3.2 DAG for Within-X Complete-Case Comparisons

We first use a causal DAG to establish when treatment comparisons within covariate strata among complete cases identify their conditional treatment effects. The next subsection then examines when regression pools these comparisons correctly.

Consider complete cases with the same pre-treatment covariate values Xi=xX_{i}=x, and let δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x) denote their average treatment effect. When both treatment arms have positive probability in this stratum, the population coefficient from regressing YiY_{i} on an intercept and DiD_{i} equals the treated-minus-control difference in mean outcomes. We show when this difference identifies δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x).

We augment the causal DAG for the oracle regression variables Yi,Di,XiY_{i},D_{i},X_{i} with the omnibus missing indicator MiM_{i} and its causes. This recasts selection on being observed, the restriction that defines complete-case regression, as selection on the observable indicator MiM_{i}, specifically Mi=0M_{i}=0. As Figure 2 illustrates, this conditioning can open noncausal paths, where {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion under mechanism B but not mechanism C.

Adjustment criterion

To assess whether {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} is a valid adjustment set, we use the criterion of Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins (2010, Definition 5), a generalization of the back-door criterion of Pearl (1995) (see also Cinelli, Forney and Pearl 2024), stated here for a single treatment DD and outcome YY.

Definition 2 (Causal missingness mechanism for listwise deletion).

Let GG be a causal DAG containing the oracle variables Yi,Di,XiY_{i},D_{i},X_{i}, the omnibus missing indicator MiM_{i}, and any other relevant observed or latent causes. The causal missingness mechanism for listwise deletion consists of the causal relationships leading to MiM_{i} and the process determining it, while GG represents its causal structure.

Definition 3 (Adjustment criterion for a single treatment).

Let GG be a causal DAG with treatment DD, outcome YY, and a set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of variables disjoint from {D,Y}\{D,Y\}. The set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} satisfies the adjustment criterion if:

  1. 1.

    𝒵\mathcal{Z} contains no node other than DD on a directed path from DD to YY, nor any descendant of such a node1212 12 A node counts as its own descendant. Unlike the back-door criterion, the adjustment criterion can permit a descendant of DD on a branch that does not lead to YY, provided all noncausal paths are blocked. See Appendix D for the general forms..

  2. 2.

    Conditioning on 𝒵\mathcal{Z} blocks every noncausal path from DD to YY1313 13 A noncausal path is one that is not directed entirely from DD to YY (Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins 2010, Section 2).

A path is blocked given 𝒵\mathcal{Z} if it contains a noncollider in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, or a collider with neither itself nor any descendant in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} (Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins 2010, Section 2). Applying the criterion to 𝒵={Xi,Mi}\mathcal{Z}=\{X_{i},M_{i}\} gives the following result.

Proposition 1 (Adjustment criterion, conditional ignorability, and within-XX complete-case comparison).

Write δcc(x)=𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Xi=x,Mi=0]\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]. If {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion relative to (Di,Yi)(D_{i},Y_{i}) in GG, then:

  1. (i)

    in every causal model inducing GG, for each d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\},

    Yi​(d)⟂Di|Xi,Mi;Y_{i}(d)\perp D_{i}\mid X_{i},M_{i};
  2. (ii)

    for any complete-case stratum Xi=xX_{i}=x with treatment overlap, the population coefficient on DiD_{i} from regressing YiY_{i} on an intercept and DiD_{i} equals

    𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Xi=x,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Xi=x,Mi=0]=δcc(x).\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]=\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x).

    With a constant unit-level treatment effect Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)=τY_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)=\tau for every unit, δcc(x)=𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Xi=x,Mi=0]=τ\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]=\tau.

Proof in Appendix D.

The proposition shows that δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x) is identified when the covariates and missing indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion and both treatment arms are represented within each complete-case covariate stratum, which provides the foundation for aggregating the conditional effects later.

Although the criterion is formal, checking it adds little to the diagram work that already supports the oracle regression. A researcher who uses a DAG to choose its adjustment set can add the missing indicator MiM_{i} and its causes, including relevant unobserved ones, to that same diagram and ask whether the original set still works among complete cases.

3.3 Pooling Within-XX Comparisons into Regression

As mechanism B in Section 2 illustrates, valid within-covariate treatment comparisons do not ensure that the pooled regression consistently estimates the complete-case ATE. The following two propositions give sufficient conditions under which unweighted complete-case regression does so.

Proposition 2 (Correct specification and the complete-case ATE).

Suppose {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion and complete-case treatment overlap holds (Assumption A2). Consider the complete-case regression

Yi=g​(Xi)⊤​αcc+Di​h​(Xi)⊤​βcc+εcc,i,Mi=0,Y_{i}=g(X_{i})^{\top}\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}+D_{i}h(X_{i})^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i},\qquad M_{i}=0,

where g⁡(Xi)g(X_{i}) contains an intercept and the chosen baseline covariate terms, and h⁡(Xi)h(X_{i}) contains an intercept and the chosen terms interacted with treatment. Suppose this regression is correctly specified in conditional mean:

𝔼[εcc,i∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=0.\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=0.

Then, under SUTVA (Assumption A1),

δcc​(x)=h​(x)⊤​βcc,\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=h(x)^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}},

and averaging over the complete-case covariate distribution gives the complete-case ATE, τcc\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}:

τcc≡𝔼⁡[h​(Xi)⊤​βcc∣Mi=0]=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0].\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}\equiv\mathbb{E}[h(X_{i})^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}\mid M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0].

Let β^cc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}} be the complete-case OLS estimate and nccn_{\mathrm{cc}} the number of complete cases. Under standard regularity conditions (Assumptions A3 and A4 in Appendix D),

τ^cc≡1ncc∑i:Mi=0h(Xi)⊤β^cc→𝑝τcc.\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}}\equiv\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i:M_{i}=0}h(X_{i})^{\top}\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}}\xrightarrow{p}\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

Proof in Appendix D.3.

When h⁡(Xi)=1h(X_{i})=1, there are no treatment–covariate interactions, βcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}} is a scalar, and the conditional treatment effect is the same for every XiX_{i}, so the coefficient on DiD_{i} is that common effect. Equation (2) is this no-interaction case, and Proposition 2 generalizes it by allowing βcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}} to be a vector. When interactions are included, h⁡(Xi)h(X_{i}) varies with the covariates, the coefficient on DiD_{i} alone describes only the reference group, and the complete-case ATE must be recovered by averaging the fitted conditional effects over the covariate distribution observed among complete cases.

Proposition 2 identifies two requirements for consistently estimating the complete-case ATE, τcc\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}: valid within-covariate comparisons and their correct aggregation. The adjustment criterion, together with treatment overlap, makes those comparisons causally valid. Correct specification of the complete-case outcome regression makes the aggregation valid1414 14 Proposition 2 generalizes the specification and selection argument of Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018): their indicator–error independence condition, together with correct oracle specification, implies the complete-case zero conditional mean condition required here. Our graphical condition additionally establishes the causal interpretation as the complete-case ATE, which their coefficient-preservation result does not address. See Appendix D.4 for a discussion.: it allows the fitted conditional treatment effects to be averaged over complete cases, and with the stated regularity conditions that average is consistent for τcc\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

However, correct specification after listwise deletion may be harder to establish than researchers expect. A regression correctly specified for the oracle sample may be misspecified after deletion because selection can change how the mean outcome depends on the covariates (Heckman 1979). Section 2’s Mechanism B illustrates this: a linear term for XiX_{i} is sufficient in the oracle regression, but the complete-case regression must capture a separate baseline mean for each XiX_{i} stratum. Two practical responses, a more flexible outcome model and residual diagnostics for the specification, are reserved for future work. The main takeaway from Proposition 2 is instead interpretive: whether the specification remains adequate after deletion may require assumptions about unobserved outcome determinants and how they affect missingness, beyond the determinants the oracle regression already includes.

Treatment-propensity weighting, not IPW for missingness1515 15 IPW for missingness weights complete cases by the inverse probability of being a complete case to address selection due to missingness (Seaman and White 2013; Hughes et al. 2019). Here, we weight by the inverse treatment probability among complete cases to pool their within-covariate treatment comparisons., offers another way to pool valid within-covariate comparisons without requiring a correctly specified outcome equation (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983; Hirano, Imbens and Ridder 2003). Appendix Proposition D.1 states the standard IPW result for complete cases (Hirano, Imbens and Ridder 2003; Choi, Dekkers and le Cessie 2019). Here, we consider its use in a complete-case regression.

Proposition 3 (Graphical criterion for complete-case IPW regression).

Suppose {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion and complete-case treatment overlap holds (Assumption A2).

Among complete cases, consider the IPW-weighted working regression

Yi=α+β​Di+Xi⊤​γ+εipw,i,ωi=Die0​(Xi)+1−Di1−e0​(Xi),Y_{i}=\alpha+\beta D_{i}+X_{i}^{\top}\gamma+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ipw},i},\qquad\omega_{i}=\frac{D_{i}}{e_{0}(X_{i})}+\frac{1-D_{i}}{1-e_{0}(X_{i})},

where e0​(x)=P⁡(Di=1∣Xi=x,Mi=0)e_{0}(x)=P(D_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0). Let β∗\beta^{*} denote the population counterpart of the IPW-weighted regression coefficient on DiD_{i} among complete cases. Then, under SUTVA and standard regularity conditions (Assumptions A1, A4, and A6 in Appendix D),

β∗=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0].\beta^{*}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0].

If the propensity score is estimated consistently, in the sense that the estimated inverse weights converge uniformly (Assumption A5), the sample coefficient β^\widehat{\beta}, computed using e^0\widehat{e}_{0}, converges in probability to β∗\beta^{*}.

The proposition follows from Proposition 1 and Proposition D.2, which applies Gabriel et al. (2024) to complete cases.

Among complete cases, the weights make each treatment arm reproduce the complete-case covariate distribution and set the weighted treatment probability to one-half within every supported stratum Xi=xX_{i}=x (Hernán and Robins 2020, Section 2.4). The weighted regression therefore pools the valid within-XX comparisons without the correctly specified complete-case outcome mean that Proposition 2 requires, relying instead on the estimated propensity weights.

In practice, weighting adds one input, a propensity model for treatment among complete cases. Its inverse weights are informative only where the data have treatment overlap, and the within-XX comparisons still need the adjustment criterion in the augmented DAG. As the motivating simulation shows, weighting addresses the pooling problem under mechanism B but cannot repair the invalid comparisons under mechanism C.

Corollary 1 (Constant complete-case propensity: unweighted OLS equals IPW).

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 3 hold, and additionally there exists e¯0∈(0,1)\bar{e}_{0}\in(0,1) such that e0​(x)=e¯0e_{0}(x)=\bar{e}_{0} for every xx in the complete-case support. Then, for any chosen g⁡(Xi)g(X_{i}) containing an intercept, the unweighted additive complete-case regression

Yi=g​(Xi)⊤​αcc+βcc​Di+εcc,i,Mi=0,Y_{i}=g(X_{i})^{\top}\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}+\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}D_{i}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i},\qquad M_{i}=0,

has βcc=τcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}} regardless of whether g​(Xi)⊤​αccg(X_{i})^{\top}\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}} correctly specifies the complete-case baseline mean, and, under Assumption A3, β^cc→𝑝τcc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}}\xrightarrow{p}\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}: unweighted OLS coincides with IPW whenever every complete-case unit shares the same treatment propensity.

Proof in Appendix D.6.

A constant complete-case propensity makes DiD_{i} exactly mean-independent of any function of XiX_{i} among complete cases, so adding, omitting, or misspecifying baseline controls does not affect the consistency of the treatment coefficient (Lin 2013). Unlike Proposition 2, this route does not require correctly specifying the shape of treatment-effect heterogeneity: the additive specification h⁡(Xi)=1h(X_{i})=1 recovers the complete-case ATE regardless of how δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x) varies with xx.

Finally, we show in Appendix D.3 that Propositions 1–3 still hold when treatment itself affects missingness, e.g. when treatment induces attrition.

Connection to the Oracle Target

Both regression approaches consistently estimate the complete-case ATE under their respective assumptions1616 16 The researcher’s target may be another causal estimand, such as the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT). Proposition 2 extends to the complete-case ATT by averaging the fitted conditional effects over treated complete cases. Under Corollary 1, the complete-case ATE, ATT, and ATU coincide because treatment is independent of covariates among complete cases. Proposition 3 targets the complete-case ATE, and the ATT requires different weights. Connecting any complete-case estimand to its population target requires additional assumptions.. To recover the population ATE, we also need to establish that the complete-case ATE equals the population ATE. The next subsection gives conditions for this connection under constant and heterogeneous treatment effects.

3.4 When Complete-Case Regression Recovers the Population ATE

Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, the connection is immediate: τcc=τ\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau. Either regression approach therefore consistently estimates the population ATE under its respective assumptions.

Corollary 2 (Constant unit-level treatment effect).

Suppose there is a constant treatment effect for every unit, Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)=τY_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)=\tau, and P⁡(Mi=0)>0P(M_{i}=0)>0. Then

𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0]=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)]=τ.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)]=\tau.

Under the conditions of Proposition 2, τcc=τ\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau, and τ^cc\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}} converges in probability to τ\tau.

Under the conditions of Proposition 3, β∗=τ\beta^{*}=\tau. Under Assumption A5 (estimated inverse-weight consistency), β^\widehat{\beta} also converges in probability to τ\tau.

Under the conditions of Corollary 1, βcc=τ\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau as well, and β^cc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}} converges in probability to τ\tau.

With heterogeneous effects, however, τcc\tau_{\mathrm{cc}} may not equal the population ATE, τ\tau. Recovering the latter requires connecting the effects among complete cases to those in the population.

To make that connection, we assume mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity: at every value of the covariates used for transport, the average treatment effect is the same among complete cases and in the population. Effects may still vary across those covariates. Within one value, selection need only be unrelated to the effect. This condition also relaxes the outcome-response ignorability assumption of Huang and Liu (2026).1717 17 For full-covariate transport, given valid within-XiX_{i} treatment comparisons in both the population and complete cases, outcome-response ignorability (Yang, Wang and Ding 2019; Huang and Liu 2026) is sufficient for mean exchangeability but not necessary. For example, selection on an unobserved characteristic that raises both potential outcomes equally changes their conditional means while preserving the conditional average treatment effect. This is more plausible when the observed covariates capture characteristics that influence both completeness and responses to treatment, and it may fail when an unobserved characteristic does (Egami and Hartman 2023; Chen and Huang 2026).

Corollary 3 (Heterogeneous treatment effects).

Suppose the conditions of Proposition 1 hold with adjustment covariates XiX_{i}. Let WiW_{i} be a subvector of XiX_{i}, possibly XiX_{i} itself, and let FpoWF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W} denote its population distribution. Suppose 𝔼⁡[|Yi​(d)|]<∞\mathbb{E}[|Y_{i}(d)|]<\infty for d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}. Further, suppose mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity given WiW_{i} holds: for almost every ww with respect to FpoWF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W},

𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Wi=w,Mi=0]=𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Wi=w].\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid W_{i}=w,M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid W_{i}=w].

Suppose also that P⁡(Mi=0∣Wi=w)>0P(M_{i}=0\mid W_{i}=w)>0 for almost every such ww. Define

τcc(w)=𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Wi=w,Mi=0].\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid W_{i}=w,M_{i}=0].

Then

τ=∫τcc​(w)​d​FpoW​(w).\tau=\int\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W}(w).

Under Assumptions A1 (SUTVA) and A2 (complete-case treatment overlap),

τcc​(w)=∫δcc​(x)​d​Fcc​(x∣Wi=w),\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)=\int\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\,dF_{\mathrm{cc}}(x\mid W_{i}=w),

where Fcc​(x∣Wi=w)F_{\mathrm{cc}}(x\mid W_{i}=w) is the distribution of XiX_{i} among complete cases with Wi=wW_{i}=w, and

δcc(x)=𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Xi=x,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Xi=x,Mi=0].\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0].

Proof in Appendix D.8.

Applying Corollary 3 asks researchers for one new judgment. The first requirement, valid within-XiX_{i} comparisons, is the adjustment-criterion check already made for Proposition 1, and positive complete-case probability across the support of WiW_{i} is an overlap question the data can answer. The new judgment is mean exchangeability given WiW_{i}, which data alone cannot establish. With all three in hand, researchers recover τ\tau by averaging τcc​(w)\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w) over FpoWF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W}, as Section 5 discusses. Further, the covariates used for adjustment XiX_{i} can be different from the covariate used for transport WiW_{i}. If transport covariates contain missingness, imputation as in Huang and Liu (2026) may recover their target distribution under additional assumptions.

Practical Advice

To sum up, empirical researchers can assess whether their complete-case regression recovers the population ATE by checking three boxes, as in Table 2. Box 1 asks whether within-covariate treatment comparisons remain valid after listwise deletion. Researchers who already use a DAG to justify their adjustment set need to add the missing indicator and its causes, then reassess the comparisons. Box 2 asks whether the regression appropriately aggregates those comparisons, either through a correctly specified complete-case outcome model or treatment-propensity weighting. Box 3 asks whether the complete-case effects connect to the population target. Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, the complete-case ATE equals the population ATE. With heterogeneous effects, researchers also need to assess the transport and support conditions and average the conditional effects over the population covariate distribution (Section 5). The next section shows how this framework incorporates and extends conventional guidance on complete-case regression.

4 Revisiting Conventional Guidance on Complete-Case Regression

In this Section, we first show how our framework recovers conventional guidance for missingness driven by regression covariates or the outcome. We follow Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018) in assuming correct oracle specification and their indicator–error independence condition, which together satisfy the specification requirement of Proposition 2. Our framework thus recovers their recommendations while allowing weaker specification and independence restrictions. We then use the collider–mediator dilemma to show why the justification for complete-case regression depends on the causal graph and the effect of interest.

4.1 Recovering Familiar Recommendations

To begin, we maintain treatment overlap, standard regularity conditions, and a constant unit-level treatment effect, so that valid complete-case treatment comparisons recover the population ATE through the correctly specified regression. The remaining question is whether the adjustment criterion holds after adding the missing indicator and its causes to the oracle DAG. The same graphical assessment still applies under heterogeneous effects (Subsection 3.4 and Section 5), and when researchers use the IPW-regression route of Proposition 3.

Table 3 reviews current recommendations about complete-case analysis (CCA), also known as listwise deletion, and multiple imputation, adapted from Pepinsky (2018). The pattern column identifies which variables contain missing values, while the mechanism column identifies what drives missingness. For example, the NMAR(X)(X) row describes missing values in XX whose probability of being missing depends only on XX. This row records that complete-case regression remains consistent when missingness depends on the value of the missing regressor (Arel-Bundock and Pelc 2018). We now use our augmented DAG to justify the CCA column and show that our theory reproduces the same recommendations.

Under MCAR, the missing indicator MiM_{i} is independent of the oracle outcome, treatment, and covariates. We represent it as an isolated node in the DAG, so adding MiM_{i} preserves identification by the original adjustment set.

Missingness driven by treatment and covariates

Figure 3 shows a causal structure in which missingness depends only on treatment DiD_{i} and the confounder vector XiX_{i}. The same structure represents three cases, each with a different variable missing (pattern) and the others observed, and with different MAR/NMAR classifications:

  1. 1.

    Missing outcome: YiY_{i} contains missing values, but its missingness depends only on the observed Di,XiD_{i},X_{i}. This is MAR and corresponds to the second row of Table 3.

  2. 2.

    Missing treatment: DiD_{i} contains missing values, and its own value affects missingness. This is NMAR and corresponds to the fourth row, where the table’s XX includes treatment.

  3. 3.

    Missing covariates: Some covariates in XiX_{i} contain missing values, and missingness depends on those covariates’ own values. This is also NMAR and corresponds to the fourth row.

In the original DAG, adjusting for XiX_{i} blocks the noncausal path Di←Xi→YiD_{i}\leftarrow X_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, identifying the population ATE from the oracle sample. Restricting to complete cases additionally conditions on the collider Di→Mi←XiD_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow X_{i}, opening the path Di→Mi←Xi→YiD_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow X_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, which remains blocked by adjustment for XiX_{i}. Moreover, MiM_{i} is on a separate branch from the causal path Di→YiD_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}. Thus, {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} satisfies the adjustment criterion. Under the maintained assumptions, complete-case regression thus consistently estimates the population ATE in all three cases, recovering the recommendation that missingness driven by regressors need not invalidate regression estimates, whether the mechanism is MAR or NMAR (Arel-Bundock and Pelc 2018).

Missingness driven by the outcome

Figure 4 retains the same treatment–outcome relationship and confounder, but missingness now instead depends only on YiY_{i}. This DAG likewise represents three cases with different classifications:

  1. 1.

    Missing outcome: YiY_{i} contains missing values, and missingness depends on its own value. This is NMAR and illustrates the outcome-driven selection covered by the fifth row of Table 3.

  2. 2.

    Missing treatment: DiD_{i} contains missing values, but missingness depends only on the observed YiY_{i}. This is MAR and corresponds to the third row.

  3. 3.

    Missing covariates: XiX_{i} contains missing values, but missingness depends only on the observed YiY_{i}. This is also MAR and corresponds to the third row.

Restricting to complete cases conditions on MiM_{i}, a descendant of YiY_{i} on the causal path Di→YiD_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}. Thus, {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} violates the first condition of the adjustment criterion, and complete-case regression is no longer guaranteed to consistently estimate the population ATE. This recovers the warning that outcome-driven missingness can invalidate complete-case regression (Heckman 1979), even under MAR (Arel-Bundock and Pelc 2018).1818 18 A notable exception is a logistic outcome model: if selection depends only on the outcome, the treatment log odds ratio is preserved (Prentice and Pyke 1979), but risk differences, and thus the ATE, are not.

Together, the two DAGs show that whether complete-case regression is justified depends on the missingness mechanism in the augmented DAG, rather than the missingness pattern or its MAR/NMAR classification.

4.2 The Collider–Mediator Dilemma

The preceding examples show how our framework recovers existing recommendations for complete-case regression. We now use it to examine a setting for which those recommendations provide no clear guidance: a variable that explains missingness and also mediates the treatment effect.

Rivlin-Angert, Yakter and Sheffer (2025) study the relationship between the Big Five personality traits and political attitudes using a survey of Jewish Israelis. Their original dataset contains 925 respondents. They use listwise deletion for all regressions, leaving 816 complete cases for specifications with sociodemographic controls1919 19 The OLS regressions include all five personality traits, with additional specifications controlling for gender, age group, education, and religious self-identification. . Our illustration draws on their analysis of conscientiousness and support for a two-state solution, specifically the mediating role of authoritarian tendency.

The authors do not discuss the missingness mechanism underlying their data, so we retain the 803 respondents with complete observations on all variables used in this illustration and impose additional missingness. We assume that respondents with below-average conscientiousness and above-average authoritarian tendencies have a 50% probability of having their outcome value unreported2020 20 Research on social desirability shows that respondents may conceal politically sensitive preferences, while research on survey effort links conscientiousness to careless responding (Carmines and Nassar 2021; Zamarro et al. 2018).. The missingness mechanism is therefore known in our synthetic data. In practice, researchers must enter that mechanism themselves into their augmented DAG. The left panel of Figure 5 augments the paper’s original mediation structure with the missing indicator and its assumed causes2121 21 The other personality traits and sociodemographic controls are omitted from the diagram..

Why the mediator creates a dilemma

While the original study distinguishes average direct and causal mediation effects, our illustration focuses on the total effect of conscientiousness on support for a two-state solution2222 22 The authors describe their analysis as “causal mediation analysis,” while acknowledging its suggestive nature (Rivlin-Angert, Yakter and Sheffer 2025, p. 404), so we use it here as an illustration.. Under the assumed causal structure and correct regression specification, regressing YiY_{i} on DiD_{i}, with the baseline controls but without the mediator AiA_{i}, consistently estimates this total effect.

Analyzing the dataset after listwise deletion conditions on Mi=0M_{i}=0, opening the noncausal path Di→Mi←Ai→YiD_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow A_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, on which MiM_{i} is a collider. Moreover, MiM_{i} is a descendant of the mediator AiA_{i} on the causal path Di→Ai→YiD_{i}\rightarrow A_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}, so conditioning on it violates the first condition of the adjustment criterion. Thus, in contrast to the case of the oracle sample, a regression of YiY_{i} on DiD_{i} can fail to consistently estimate the total effect.

The guidance that listwise deletion preserves the oracle regression coefficients when missingness is driven by included regressors (Arel-Bundock and Pelc 2018) may tempt researchers to add AiA_{i} to the regression. Indeed, adjusting for AiA_{i} blocks the opened noncausal path, but it also blocks the mediated causal path. Thus, adding the mediator to the complete-case regression does not restore identification of the total effect. The treatment coefficient, instead, identifies the controlled direct effect, which equals the average direct effect when the specification has no treatment–mediator interaction, under sequential ignorability (Imai, Keele and Tingley 2010).

Illustration with Synthetic Data

To demonstrate this, we draw 10,000 bootstrap samples of 803 respondents each, sampling with replacement from the complete-case dataset. In each sample, we impose the specified missing mechanism using the sample means of conscientiousness and authoritarian tendency as the thresholds. Specifically,

Pr⁡(Mi=1∣Di,Ai)={0.5,Di<D¯​and​Ai>A¯,0,otherwise.\Pr(M_{i}=1\mid D_{i},A_{i})=\begin{cases}0.5,&D_{i}<\overline{D}\ \text{and}\ A_{i}>\overline{A},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

On average, 11.5 percent of outcomes are missing. In each bootstrap sample, we estimate the following models, all of which include the authors’ sociodemographic controls.

  • •

    Oracle estimator: regress YiY_{i} on DiD_{i}, without the mediator AiA_{i}, on the oracle dataset before imposing missingness.

  • •

    Oracle with AiA_{i} (Oracle + A): regress YiY_{i} on DiD_{i} and AiA_{i} on the oracle dataset.

  • •

    Complete-case estimator (CCA): regress YiY_{i} on DiD_{i}, without AiA_{i}, on the complete-case dataset where Mi=0M_{i}=0.

  • •

    Complete-case estimator with AiA_{i} (CCA + A): regress YiY_{i} on DiD_{i} and AiA_{i} after listwise deletion.

  • •

    Multiple-imputation estimator (MI): impute missing YiY_{i} using DiD_{i}, AiA_{i}, and the baseline controls, then regress YiY_{i} on DiD_{i}, without AiA_{i}, on the imputed datasets and pool the estimates (Little and Rubin 2019).

Figure 6 summarizes the empirical distributions of these estimators. Neither CCA nor CCA + A is centered around the oracle total-effect benchmark of −0.560-0.5602323 23 Our oracle regressions yield total- and controlled-direct-effect estimates of −0.560-0.560 and −0.305-0.305, compared with −0.564-0.564 and −0.310-0.310 in Rivlin-Angert, Yakter and Sheffer (2025, Table 4). The small differences arise because they report averages over 1,000 quasi-Bayesian draws, while we report OLS point estimates.. Instead, CCA + A is concentrated near the oracle controlled direct-effect benchmark of −0.305-0.305. These results are consistent with the predictions from the augmented DAG.

We also observe that the multiple-imputation estimates are centered near the oracle total-effect benchmark of −0.560-0.560. This is consistent with the imposed MAR mechanism: missingness depends only on observed conscientiousness and authoritarian tendency. Multiple imputation enables researchers to include both variables and the baseline controls in the imputation model while keeping the mediator out of the total-effect regression2424 24 We analyze the canonical listwise-deletion workflow. G-computation could instead recover the total effect under suitable assumptions by combining a complete-case outcome model with the mediator distribution conditional on treatment and baseline controls, estimated from the original sample..

When authoritarian tendency is a confounder

We now consider an alternative substantive theory in which authoritarian tendency is a confounder of the relationship between conscientiousness and support for a two-state solution. Political science research sometimes treats authoritarianism as a relatively enduring predisposition that shapes political attitudes (Stenner 2005; Engelhardt, Feldman and Hetherington 2023). The right panel of Figure 5 represents this alternative causal structure, retaining the same missing mechanism.

The missingness mechanism is MAR in both left and right DAGs, but the causal role of AiA_{i} differs, as shown by the reversed arrow between DiD_{i} and AiA_{i}. When AiA_{i} is a confounder, conditioning on MiM_{i} opens the noncausal path Di→Mi←Ai→YiD_{i}\rightarrow M_{i}\leftarrow A_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}. Adjusting for AiA_{i} blocks both this path and the original back-door path Di←Ai→YiD_{i}\leftarrow A_{i}\rightarrow Y_{i}. Under the maintained identification and regression-specification assumptions, complete-case regression adjusting for AiA_{i} therefore consistently estimates the total effect. Consistent with the augmented DAG, Figure 7 shows that CCA + A is centered near the total-effect benchmark of −0.305-0.3052525 25 The oracle regression adjusting for authoritarian tendency yields the same coefficient, −0.305-0.305, as in the mediation illustration, but it identifies the total effect under the confounder DAG. CCA + A averages −0.285-0.285 because, in the finite sample used for the bootstrap, respondents subject to missingness happen to lie slightly above the fitted line – deleting some flattens the slope. This offset would vanish as the original sample grows if the population conditional mean of the outcome is linear in authoritarian tendency..

In this illustration, we show that the same dataset, missingness pattern, and MAR classification may call for different strategies under different causal structures. Adjusting for authoritarian tendency identifies the total effect when it is a confounder, but blocks part of that effect when it is a mediator. Different causal structures can generate observationally equivalent data, so researchers must specify their causal assumptions to assess whether complete-case analysis remains justified after conditioning on the missing indicator. Appendix E further supplies a separate simulation of the dilemma, including missing-outcome and missing-treatment cases.

5 Reweighting Complete-Case Comparisons: Heterogeneous Effects

In this section, we extend the framework to heterogeneous treatment effects by reweighting complete-case comparisons to recover population averages. Appendix F further applies the same approach to generalized linear models.

5.1 Reweighting for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

Let WiW_{i} denote the covariates used for transport in Corollary 3. Let δcc​(w)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w) and δpo​(w)\delta_{\mathrm{po}}(w) denote the conditional average treatment effects among complete cases and in the population, respectively. Let FccF_{\mathrm{cc}} and FpoF_{\mathrm{po}} denote the distributions of WiW_{i} among complete cases and in the population. Then

τcc=∫δcc​(w)​d​Fcc​(w),τ=∫δpo​(w)​d​Fpo​(w).\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\int\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{cc}}(w),\qquad\tau=\int\delta_{\mathrm{po}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{po}}(w).

Under mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity, δcc​(w)=δpo​(w)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)=\delta_{\mathrm{po}}(w) for almost every ww with respect to FpoF_{\mathrm{po}}. With complete-case support, we therefore have

τcc−τ=∫δcc​(w)​d​Fcc​(w)−∫δcc​(w)​d​Fpo​(w).\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}-\tau=\int\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)-\int\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{po}}(w).

Under these conditions, the difference arises from averaging the same conditional treatment effects over different covariate distributions. This decomposition also situates the two-stage projection estimator of Huang and Liu (2026). In the full-covariate case Wi=XiW_{i}=X_{i}, their outcome-response ignorability and treatment-identification conditions imply δcc​(w)=δpo​(w)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)=\delta_{\mathrm{po}}(w). As some confounders are missing, they estimate outcome models among complete cases, impute missing covariates such that they can project the fitted models onto the completed covariate data to average predicted conditional effects over the full sample.

Our framework generalizes this identification argument by specifying graphical conditions under which complete-case comparisons identify δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x) (Proposition 1). It also generalizes the transport step in two ways: mean exchangeability allows selection to change conditional outcome means as long as the conditional treatment effect is preserved, and the transport covariates WiW_{i} may be a subvector of the adjustment covariates XiX_{i}. Rather than first pooling these comparisons into the complete-case ATE, τcc\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}, through the regression approaches in Propositions 2 and 3, Corollary 3 provides a direct route to the population ATE: given identified within-XiX_{i} effects, average δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x) over the complete-case distribution of XiX_{i} within each Wi=wW_{i}=w group, then average the resulting effects over the population distribution of WiW_{i}, assuming mean exchangeability and complete-case support given WiW_{i}.

The identification results also allow continuous moderators, but implementing the population-averaging result in that setting requires additional assumptions about how conditional effects are estimated, which we have not developed here. The reanalysis in Subsection 5.2 instead uses categorical moderators, for which the averaging step is explicit.

5.2 Reanalysis of Bodea and Hicks (2015)

Bodea and Hicks (2015) study the conditional effects of central bank independence (CBI) using data on 78 countries from 1973 to 2008. They find that CBI lowers inflation in democracies but not in nondemocracies. Their country fixed-effects regressions interact the CBI index with six measures of democracy and democratic institutions: Polity (Marshall and Gurr 2020), Freedom House (Freedom House 2021), executive constraints (Marshall and Gurr 2020), checks and balances (Cruz, Keefer and Scartascini 2021), political constraints (Henisz 2000; Henisz 2012), and press freedom (Freedom House 2017).

We reanalyze their study using the authors’ updated and expanded CBI data, which cover 143 countries and the European Central Bank from 1970 to 2020 (Bodea and Hicks 2023), along with updated data from the original sources of the moderators. For 1973–2008, the expanded data contain 132 countries with CBI and Polity observed, of which 115 (2,198 country-years) have every control observed. The outcome is signed log inflation, and effects are reported per 0.1 increase in the CBI index. Without a moderator, we reproduce the authors’ original CBI coefficient of −0.465-0.465 (SE 0.143) per unit of CBI. The expanded data yield −0.546-0.546 (Figure 8, leftmost panel).

In the original data, 2,061 country-years in 79 countries have CBI and Polity observed during the analysis period. After listwise deletion, 1,769 country-years in 78 countries enter the authors’ baseline regression. Our main comparison concerns heterogeneous effects in the expanded data, retaining the economic controls and country fixed effects. To account for possible nonlinearity in the moderating effects (Hainmueller, Mummolo and Xu 2019), we divide each measure into three categories and fit a country fixed-effects regression within each. Holding these category-specific estimates fixed, we compare their averages using complete-case and target-population shares (Table G1, Panel B). Although CBI is continuous, the population-averaging result in Corollary 3 can be extended to category-specific CBI slopes, taking their causal interpretation and consistent estimation as given2626 26 The arguments in Propositions 1–2 and Corollary 3 can be adapted to continuous treatments. A sufficient DGP is Yi​t​(d)=ai,w+μw​(Hi​t)+sw​d+ui​tY_{it}(d)=a_{i,w}+\mu_{w}(H_{it})+s_{w}d+u_{it}, where ww is a pretreatment moderator category and Hi​tH_{it} contains pretreatment controls and outcome history. Under valid adjustment, treatment support, consistency, no interference, and a correctly specified complete-case conditional mean, sws_{w} is the category-specific causal slope. If these slopes transport to the target categories, averaging 0.1​sw0.1s_{w} using target shares gives the target average effect per 0.1 increase in CBI..

Bodea and Hicks (2015) do not specify a missingness mechanism for their main regression variables. To focus the illustration for Box 3, we assume their complete-case regression uses a valid adjustment set and is correctly specified. In the compatible causal structure in Figure 3, missingness is driven by treatment and covariates, and treatment comparisons within covariate strata remain valid among complete cases. By granting these conditions, we show that even valid complete-case comparisons may not recover the population ATE when treatment effects vary and listwise deletion changes the distribution of moderators.

Following Corollary 3, with the moderator as WiW_{i}, we assume mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity2727 27 Here, we assume that each category’s fixed-effects slope equals its complete-case average effect, which in turn equals its target-population average. For example, under Polity, only 11 of the 38 complete-case autocracies have within-country CBI variation. The slope identified from these 11 countries must therefore represent the average effect across all complete-case autocracies and, under mean exchangeability, all target-population autocracies.: the average effect within each moderator category is the same among complete cases and in the target population, in addition to complete-case support. We then hold the estimated category-specific effects fixed and average them using their population shares to recover the population average.

Whereas Bodea and Hicks (2015) focus on the conditional effects themselves, we consider a case in which researchers are concerned with the population ATE. Suppose the target population consists of country-years in the countries covered by the expanded CBI data. As Figure 8 shows, for three of the six moderators, the complete-case average is negative and statistically significant, whereas the average reweighted to the target population’s moderator distribution is not statistically distinguishable from zero. For four of the six moderators, the difference between the complete-case and reweighted averages is statistically significant at the 5% level using unadjusted pp-values.

This is because listwise deletion changes the moderator distribution: democracies and countries with stronger democratic institutions are overrepresented among complete cases2828 28 As Panel C of Table G1 shows, in the expanded data, democracies account for 67.2% of complete-case country-years, while the corresponding share among country-years in the target population is 48.4%., so the complete-case average places more weight on effects in these categories than the population average. Interpreting the complete-case average as a population average can therefore be misleading. The same pattern also holds when the target population is all country-years covered by Polity5, a larger population than the country-years in countries covered by the expanded CBI data. Table G1 reports the numerical results.

6 Checking All Three Boxes: Complete-Case Analysis in a Canvassing Experiment

The preceding two sections illustrate the use of DAGs and reweighting to assess complete-case regression. We now reanalyze Kalla and Broockman (2023) to show how researchers can justify listwise deletion through all three checks: the validity of treatment comparisons using a DAG, the pooling of those comparisons through treatment weighting, and reweighting to recover the population ATE.

Their Study 1 examines whether canvassing conversations reduce prejudice toward undocumented immigrants. We compare their full intervention, which used personal stories and perspective-taking, with a placebo conversation on an unrelated topic, and use their first-follow-up outcome index, measured approximately one week after canvassing. Among the 1,900 participants in these two arms, 728 (38.3 percent) have no observed first-follow-up outcome, leaving 1,172 complete cases. Treatment assignment, baseline education, and the regression controls are fully observed. The missing pattern is purely on the follow-up outcomes: 45.0 percent of participants without a college degree and 30.9 percent of those with one lack the outcome.

Box 1: Do Treatment Comparisons Remain Valid after Listwise Deletion?

Let DD denote assignment to the full intervention rather than the placebo, WW baseline college education, XX the remaining baseline controls, and YY the first-follow-up outcome. Together, (W,X)(W,X) form the pretreatment covariate vector, the XX in the general framework. Let M=1M=1 indicate that YY is missing. We consider two possible missing mechanisms, represented by two DAGs in Figure 9.

In the left panel of Figure 9, missingness has three causes: treatment DD, baseline college education WW, and the remaining baseline controls XX, which include prior immigration attitudes. College-educated participants may be more likely to answer an emailed follow-up survey, and the canvassing itself may change willingness to respond2929 29 The authors find no evidence of differential attrition: follow-up response is 61.28% in the placebo arm and 62.09% in the treatment arm. We further test whether response depends on treatment conditional on education and the other baseline controls. In a linear probability model with treatment–covariate interactions, a household-clustered Wald test jointly rejects the treatment and interaction terms (χ2​(36)=61.28\chi^{2}(36)=61.28, p=0.0054p=0.0054). This evidence favors allowing D→MD\rightarrow M..

Alternatively, we may believe that follow-up response further depends on post-treatment attitudes. For example, among participants with the same baseline characteristics, those who would express less favorable attitudes toward undocumented immigrants might be less willing to respond. This adds the arrow Y→MY\rightarrow M, shown in the right panel of Figure 9.

In the left panel, conditioning on the collider MM opens the noncausal paths D→M←W→YD\rightarrow M\leftarrow W\rightarrow Y and D→M←X→YD\rightarrow M\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y. Adjusting for WW and XX blocks both paths. Moreover, MM is not a descendant of a node on the causal path, so the adjustment criterion in Proposition 1 is satisfied. In the right panel, MM is a descendant of YY on the causal path D→YD\rightarrow Y. Conditioning on MM therefore violates the first requirement of the adjustment criterion, so complete-case comparisons are no longer justified by Proposition 1.

Thus, under the left DAG, Box 1 is checked. Under the right DAG, there is no guarantee for valid treatment comparisons under listwise deletion, and researchers need to consider alternative strategies. In the rest of this illustration, we focus on the left DAG.

Box 2: Does the Regression Appropriately Pool the Treatment Comparisons?

We next assess whether the regression appropriately pools treatment comparisons within baseline-covariate strata into the complete-case ATE. The authors randomly assigned households within blocks, with equal probabilities of assignment to each arm3030 30 For this application, we assume i.i.d. sampling of households rather than individuals, in which consistency still holds under regularity conditions.. Under the left panel of the DAG, treatment and baseline characteristics jointly determine whether the follow-up outcome is missing, so the complete-case treatment propensity may vary across baseline-covariate strata. We therefore use treatment IPW under Proposition 3 to pool the comparisons, estimating treatment probabilities among complete cases with a probit model including education and other baseline controls.

The IPW estimate is 0.0932 (Table H1). We also estimate complete-case effects separately within each education group, fitting a separate treatment propensity model and treatment-IPW regression in each group. The estimates are 0.0497 for participants without a college degree and 0.1107 for those with one. We use these education-specific estimates for reweighting below.

Box 3: Does the Complete-Case Regression Recover the Population ATE?

Having checked Boxes 1 and 2, we ask whether a complete-case regression that omits the education moderator recovers the population ATE. When effects vary by education, the complete-case ATE averages conditional effects over the education distribution among complete cases, whereas the population ATE averages population conditional effects over the population distribution (Corollary 3).

Suppose mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity holds at the level of education, so that within each education group the average treatment effect is the same among complete cases and in the population. If complete cases are represented in every population education group, we can estimate the population ATE by averaging the complete-case education-specific effects using the population shares. Here, population refers to the popuation represented by the 1,900 participants under original authors’ recruitment and sampling procedure.

In the data, college-educated participants account for 53.2% of complete cases, but 47.5% of the target sample. Averaging the education-specific effects using the target shares yields 0.0787, compared3131 31 This comparison captures both treatment IPW and reweighting by education. Using the same education-specific estimates, changing from complete-case to target shares gives a difference of −0.0035-0.0035. with 0.0925 from the pooled complete-case regression. Their difference is −0.0138-0.0138, with a 95% paired household-bootstrap interval of [−0.0488,0.0174][-0.0488,0.0174].

Thus, reweighting to the population share does not produce a statistically significant change in the estimated effect. This is partly due to the fact that the treatment effect does not statistically differ by education (p=0.281p=0.281, two-sided household bootstrap). If treatment effects do differ, however, the statistically insignificant difference between the complete-case and reweighted estimates in this finite sample does not establish that the complete-case estimator converges to the population ATE.
