The difference between the education distributions of complete cases and the population also would not disappear as the sample size grows, so does the resulting difference in averaging weights.

7 Concluding Remarks

This article asks when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect. It does so when complete-case treatment comparisons identify the relevant conditional effects (under the adjustment criterion and treatment overlap) and the regression estimator pools those comparisons appropriately (through correct specification or IPW). With heterogeneous effects, recovering the population ATE also requires averaging the conditional effects over the population covariate distribution. Most importantly, MAR or NMAR labels alone do not establish these conditions.

Our framework brings existing guidance on complete-case regression into an augmented causal diagram. Recommendations for missingness driven by covariates or the outcome follow as special cases, while differences between Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018) and Pepinsky (2018) reflect different assumptions about the missingness mechanism and regression specification. The collider–mediator illustration shows why MAR labels alone cannot determine whether listwise deletion is justified: with the same data, missing pattern, and MAR classification, adjusting for authoritarian tendency recovers the total effect when it is a confounder, but not when it is a mediator. Because these causal structures can be observationally equivalent, researchers must state the assumptions they use to justify listwise deletion, just as they do when choosing an adjustment set for the oracle regression.

For empirical researchers, Table 2 summarizes the checks: start with the oracle regression’s adjustment set, which would identify the population ATE, assess treatment comparisons in its augmented DAG, verify that the estimator pools them appropriately, and, with heterogeneous effects, average conditional effects over the target population’s covariate distribution. Our Bodea–Hicks reanalysis illustrates that a negative, statistically significant complete-case average can become indistinguishable from zero after reweighting. In the canvassing reanalysis, the complete-case and reweighted estimates are not statistically distinguishable, but this finite-sample result does not establish consistency: any population gap caused by averaging over the wrong distribution persists as the sample grows. Our framework gives researchers a formal basis for assessing listwise deletion and its consequences. By making the assumed causes of missingness explicit, researchers can explain when deletion is appropriate for their causal question.

When the conditions cannot be established, researchers have two broad options. They may turn to methods that address the missing part of the data, such as imputation or IPW for missingness, and assess the assumptions those methods require. Alternatively, they may retain listwise deletion and use bounds or sensitivity analysis to assess what can be learned when the conditions for complete-case regression are uncertain.

Thus, several limitations and possible extensions remain. First, future work could develop bounds and sensitivity analyses for settings where the conditions for complete-case regression are uncertain, as well as diagnostics for the outcome specification. Second, our framework could be extended to other causal estimands, such as the ATT and the complier average treatment effect, and to estimation and inference with continuous treatment-effect modifiers. Software could also help researchers construct augmented causal diagrams and assess whether they satisfy the graphical conditions for valid complete-case comparisons. Finally, we note that even when complete-case regression is consistent, the number of complete observations can become very small as the number of variables with missing values grows (Wang and Aronow 2023). In such cases, consistency provides limited assurance for the available sample, and imputation may be needed to use information from incomplete observations.

Appendix A Review of Missing Data in APSR and AJPS, 2019–2024

To approximate Huang and Liu (2026), we screened 2019–2024 Crossref records for causal terms, such as causal, effect of, and confound, and excluded records mentioning experimental designs. We chose this rule partly to approximate their sample sizes before full-text eligibility review. Full-text eligibility review retained 100 APSR and 58 AJPS observational causal studies.

Claude Opus 5.5 coded ten pilot articles, and Claude Sonnet 5 coded the remaining articles’ main texts and available appendices. We reviewed the AI-generated coding using the same standards we apply to work produced by a human research assistant and found the results reliable. We asked the agent to code deletion as stated when named and implied when missing values were given as the reason for dropping observations, while not to count unexplained sample-size differences. Table A1 summarizes the results.

Appendix B Numerical Results for the Motivating Simulation

B.1 Saturated Regression and IPW under Mechanisms B and C

Recall the within-XiX_{i} complete-case model from the main text, Yi=αXi+βXi​Di+εstr,iY_{i}=\alpha_{X_{i}}+\beta_{X_{i}}D_{i}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{str},i}. Here βx\beta_{x} is the observed treated-minus-untreated contrast at Xi=xX_{i}=x. For both mechanisms, the Complete case, saturated XX row in Table B1 estimates, among Mi=0M_{i}=0 cases, the unweighted regression

Yi=αXisat+βsat​Di+risat,Mi=0.Y_{i}=\alpha^{\mathrm{sat}}_{X_{i}}+\beta_{\mathrm{sat}}D_{i}+r_{i}^{\mathrm{sat}},\qquad M_{i}=0.

The fitted intercept αXisat\alpha^{\mathrm{sat}}_{X_{i}} varies across the three values of XiX_{i}, while βsat\beta_{\mathrm{sat}} is common to them. risatr_{i}^{\mathrm{sat}} is the regression residual. The simulation implements these intercepts with XiX_{i}, 𝟏{Xi=−1}\mathbf{1}\{X_{i}=-1\}, and 𝟏{Xi=1}\mathbf{1}\{X_{i}=1\}. In our DGP, one of these terms is dropped because of perfect collinearity.

The Complete case with IPW row estimates the weighted regression

Yi=αIPW+βIPW​Di+γIPW​Xi+riIPW,Mi=0,Y_{i}=\alpha_{\mathrm{IPW}}+\beta_{\mathrm{IPW}}D_{i}+\gamma_{\mathrm{IPW}}X_{i}+r_{i}^{\mathrm{IPW}},\qquad M_{i}=0,

with ωi=1/e^0​(Xi)\omega_{i}=1/\hat{e}_{0}(X_{i}) for treated units and ωi=1/[1−e^0​(Xi)]\omega_{i}=1/[1-\hat{e}_{0}(X_{i})] for untreated units. e^0​(x)\hat{e}_{0}(x) is the treated proportion among complete cases with Xi=xX_{i}=x, truncated to [0.01,0.99][0.01,0.99] before weighting. riIPWr_{i}^{\mathrm{IPW}} is the regression residual.

The two mean treatment coefficients in Table B1 agree under B: 1.0021.002 for saturated OLS and 1.0021.002 for IPW. Under C, they differ: 1.5411.541 and 1.5801.580, respectively.

To explain the difference, let e0​(x)=P⁡(Di=1∣Xi=x,Mi=0)e_{0}(x)=P(D_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0). In the population, the two coefficients pool the βx\beta_{x} contrasts as

IPW:\displaystyle\text{IPW:} ∑xP⁡(X=x∣M=0)​βx,\displaystyle\sum_{x}P(X=x\mid M=0)\,\beta_{x},
Saturated-X OLS:\displaystyle\text{Saturated-}X\text{ OLS:} ∑xP⁡(X=x∣M=0)​e0​(x)​[1−e0​(x)]​βx∑xP⁡(X=x∣M=0)​e0​(x)​[1−e0​(x)].\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{x}P(X=x\mid M=0)e_{0}(x)[1-e_{0}(x)]\,\beta_{x}}{\sum_{x}P(X=x\mid M=0)e_{0}(x)[1-e_{0}(x)]}.

Thus, saturated-XX OLS weights each stratum by the within-stratum variance of treatment as well as its complete-case frequency (Angrist and Pischke 2009). Under B, βx=1\beta_{x}=1 for every xx, so the different weights produce the same population coefficient. Under C, (β−1,β0,β1)=(2,1,2)(\beta_{-1},\beta_{0},\beta_{1})=(2,1,2), so the weights produce different coefficients.

Appendix C MAR Companion to the Motivating Simulation

We retain the outcome process, treatment assignment, and regression from Section 2. The oracle sample has 20,000 observations, Yi=Di+Xi+Ui+ξiY_{i}=D_{i}+X_{i}+U_{i}+\xi_{i}, and a constant unit-level treatment effect τ=1\tau=1. We add an always-observed pretreatment noisy proxy X~i=Xi+Ui+νi\widetilde{X}_{i}=X_{i}+U_{i}+\nu_{i}, where νi∼N⁡(0,0.252)\nu_{i}\sim N(0,0.25^{2}). Only XiX_{i} can be missing.

Let Mi=0M_{i}=0 when XiX_{i} is observed. We consider three mechanisms:

A:P(Mi=0∣Di,X~i)\displaystyle\text{A:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid D_{i},\widetilde{X}_{i}) =0.875−0.30​Di,\displaystyle=0.875-0.30D_{i},
B:P(Mi=0∣Di,X~i)\displaystyle\text{B:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid D_{i},\widetilde{X}_{i}) =κ 1{X~i≥−1.5},\displaystyle=\kappa\,\mathbf{1}\{\widetilde{X}_{i}\geq-1.5\},
C:P(Mi=0∣Di,X~i)\displaystyle\text{C:}\quad P(M_{i}=0\mid D_{i},\widetilde{X}_{i}) ={p0,Di=0,κ 1{X~i≥−1.5},Di=1.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}p_{0},&D_{i}=0,\\ \kappa\,\mathbf{1}\{\widetilde{X}_{i}\geq-1.5\},&D_{i}=1.\end{cases}

The constants κ≃0.9000\kappa\simeq 0.9000 and p0≃0.6946p_{0}\simeq 0.6946 give a 25% missingness rate under each mechanism. All three are MAR because observation depends only on the fully observed DiD_{i} and X~i\widetilde{X}_{i}. As in Section 2, we report complete-case regression and treatment IPW; we also report linear and correctly specified multiple imputation (MI)3232 32 Linear MI uses a multinomial-logit model for XiX_{i} with linear predictors DiD_{i}, YiY_{i}, and X~i\widetilde{X}_{i}. Correctly specified MI adds log⁡cosh⁡{(Yi−Di−x)/0.52+(X~i−x)/0.252}\log\cosh\{(Y_{i}-D_{i}-x)/0.5^{2}+(\widetilde{X}_{i}-x)/0.25^{2}\} for x∈{−1,0,1}x\in\{-1,0,1\}. Both use 20 imputations..

Figure C2 shows the same progression as the NMAR simulation. Moving from A to B illustrates the need to pool valid within-XiX_{i} comparisons appropriately; moving from B to C shows how the adjustment criterion can fail. Correctly specified MI remains centered near the target under all three MAR mechanisms, although linear MI misses the target under B.

Appendix D Technical Definitions, Assumptions, and Proofs

D.1 Adjustment criterion

Adjustment criterion in the original paper

Definition 5 of Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins (2010) defines the adjustment criterion as follows, using 𝐃\mathbf{D} for their treatment set XX to distinguish it from our covariates XiX_{i}. Let GG be a causal DAG, and let 𝐃\mathbf{D}, 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be pairwise disjoint sets of treatment, outcome, and observed adjustment variables. Let G𝐃¯G_{\overline{\mathbf{D}}} denote the graph obtained by deleting all arrows into nodes in 𝐃\mathbf{D}. A directed path from 𝐃\mathbf{D} to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} is proper if its only treatment node is its starting node. The set 𝒵\mathcal{Z} satisfies the adjustment criterion relative to (𝐃,𝐘)(\mathbf{D},\mathbf{Y}) in GG if:

  1. 1.

    In G𝐃¯G_{\overline{\mathbf{D}}}, no member of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} may descend from a node v∉𝐃v\notin\mathbf{D} that lies on a proper causal path from 𝐃\mathbf{D} to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} in GG.

  2. 2.

    𝒵\mathcal{Z} blocks every noncausal path from 𝐃\mathbf{D} to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} in GG.

A node counts as its own descendant. A noncausal path is one that is not directed from its treatment endpoint to its outcome endpoint.

Condition 1 with a single treatment

Our analysis has one treatment DD and one outcome YY, so every directed path from DD to YY is proper. For any node v≠Dv\neq D on such a path, no directed path from vv to a descendant can pass through DD, because that would create a cycle. Deleting arrows into DD therefore leaves the descendants of vv unchanged:

DeGD¯⁡(v)=DeG⁡(v).\operatorname{De}_{G_{\bar{D}}}(v)=\operatorname{De}_{G}(v).

Condition 1 thus excludes nodes other than DD on directed paths from DD to YY, together with their descendants in the original DAG.

Condition 2 with a single treatment

Condition 2 is unchanged: 𝒵\mathcal{Z} must block every noncausal path from DD to YY in the original graph GG, as stated in Section 3.

D.2 SUTVA, Oracle Samples, Missing Mechanism, and Proof of Proposition 1

Assumption A1 (Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)).

Each treatment level has a single outcome-relevant version. Let 𝐝=(d1,…,dn)\mathbf{d}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}) be a treatment assignment vector. For every unit ii and every 𝐝\mathbf{d}, the unit’s potential outcome depends only on its own assignment: Yi​(𝐝)=Yi​(di)Y_{i}(\mathbf{d})=Y_{i}(d_{i}). For the realized assignment, Yi=Yi​(Di)Y_{i}=Y_{i}(D_{i}).

Definition 4 (Oracle potential-outcome sample and oracle sample).

Let Yi​(d)Y_{i}(d) be unit ii’s potential outcome under treatment d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}. The oracle potential-outcome sample is

𝒮po={(Yi(0),Yi(1),Di,Xi,𝐌i):i=1,…,n},(Yi(0),Yi(1),Di,Xi,𝐌i)∼i.i.d.Ppo,\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{po}}=\{(Y_{i}(0),Y_{i}(1),D_{i},X_{i},\mathbf{M}_{i}):i=1,\ldots,n\},\qquad(Y_{i}(0),Y_{i}(1),D_{i},X_{i},\mathbf{M}_{i})\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}P_{\mathrm{po}},

where PpoP_{\mathrm{po}} is the joint population distribution of the respective unit-level vector.

Under SUTVA, let Yi=Yi​(Di)Y_{i}=Y_{i}(D_{i}) denote unit ii’s realized outcome. The oracle sample is

𝒮or={(Yi,Di,Xi,𝐌i):i=1,…,n},(Yi,Di,Xi,𝐌i)∼i.i.d.Por,\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{or}}=\{(Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i},\mathbf{M}_{i}):i=1,\ldots,n\},\qquad(Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i},\mathbf{M}_{i})\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}P_{\mathrm{or}},

where PorP_{\mathrm{or}} is the joint distribution induced by PpoP_{\mathrm{po}} and Yi=Yi​(Di)Y_{i}=Y_{i}(D_{i}). The sample contains every unit’s realized values, including those missing in the observed data, and retains each unit’s missing pattern.

Missing mechanism

Definition 5 (Missing mechanism).

The missing mechanism specifies the conditional probability of each missing pattern given the full realized data:

π⁡(𝐦∣y,d,x)=P⁡(𝐌i=𝐦∣Yi=y,Di=d,Xi=x).\pi(\mathbf{m}\mid y,d,x)=P(\mathbf{M}_{i}=\mathbf{m}\mid Y_{i}=y,D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x).
Assumption A2 (Complete-case treatment overlap).

Let e0​(x)=P⁡(Di=1∣Xi=x,Mi=0)e_{0}(x)=P(D_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0). For every xx in the complete-case support, 0<e0​(x)<10<e_{0}(x)<1.

Proof of Proposition 1(i).

Apply Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins (2010, Theorem 4) with their treatment XX equal to DiD_{i} and their adjustment set ZZ equal to {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\}. Their intervention-defined counterfactual YxY_{x} is our potential outcome Yi​(d)Y_{i}(d) when x=dx=d. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1(ii).

Fix a supported complete-case stratum Xi=x,Mi=0X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0 satisfying treatment overlap. The first equality follows from consistency, Yi=Yi​(Di)Y_{i}=Y_{i}(D_{i}), which means that a unit assigned dd has realized outcome Yi​(d)Y_{i}(d), while the second follows from Proposition 1(i):

𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0] =𝔼[Yi(d)∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(d)\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]
=𝔼[Yi(d)∣Xi=x,Mi=0].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(d)\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0].

Subtracting the expressions for d=1d=1 and d=0d=0 gives

𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Xi=x,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Xi=x,Mi=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]
=𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Xi=x,Mi=0]=δcc(x).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]=\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x).

Because DiD_{i} is binary, the population coefficient in a regression on an intercept and DiD_{i} within this stratum equals this difference in means. Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, δcc​(x)=τ\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=\tau. ∎

D.3 Proof of Proposition 2

Assumption A3 (Complete-case OLS regularity).

Let Zi=(g​(Xi)⊤,Di​h​(Xi)⊤)⊤Z_{i}=(g(X_{i})^{\top},D_{i}h(X_{i})^{\top})^{\top}, where gg and hh are fixed finite-dimensional vectors of chosen terms, each including an intercept. For the additive specification, take g⁡(Xi)=b⁡(Xi)g(X_{i})=b(X_{i}) and h⁡(Xi)=1h(X_{i})=1. Suppose P⁡(Mi=0)>0P(M_{i}=0)>0,

𝔼⁡[Yi2+‖Zi‖2+‖h⁡(Xi)‖2∣Mi=0]<∞,\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}^{2}+\|Z_{i}\|^{2}+\|h(X_{i})\|^{2}\mid M_{i}=0]<\infty,

and G0=𝔼⁡[Zi​Zi⊤∣Mi=0]G_{0}=\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top}\mid M_{i}=0] is positive definite.

Proof of Proposition 2.

Correct specification of the complete-case conditional mean gives

𝔼[Yi∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=g(Xi)⊤αcc+Dih(Xi)⊤βcc.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=g(X_{i})^{\top}\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}+D_{i}h(X_{i})^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

Under Assumption A2 (complete-case treatment overlap), both treatment arms have positive probability at each supported Xi=xX_{i}=x. Subtracting their conditional means cancels the baseline term g​(x)⊤​αccg(x)^{\top}\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}, giving

𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Xi=x,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Xi=x,Mi=0]=h(x)⊤βcc.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]=h(x)^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

By SUTVA (Assumption A1), a unit assigned dd has realized outcome Yi​(d)Y_{i}(d). The adjustment criterion then makes the comparison causal, as established in Proposition 1(ii). Hence

δcc​(x)=h​(x)⊤​βcc.\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=h(x)^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

Averaging over Xi|Mi=0X_{i}\mid M_{i}=0 and applying the law of iterated expectations gives

𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0]=𝔼⁡[h​(Xi)⊤​βcc∣Mi=0]=τcc.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[h(X_{i})^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}\mid M_{i}=0]=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

The integrability needed for this averaging follows from Assumption A4.

For consistency, let ϑcc=(αcc⊤,βcc⊤)⊤\vartheta_{\mathrm{cc}}=(\alpha_{\mathrm{cc}}^{\top},\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}^{\top})^{\top}. Multiplying the zero conditional residual mean by ZiZ_{i} and averaging gives the complete-case population OLS normal equations:

𝔼⁡[Zi​(Yi−Zi⊤​ϑcc)∣Mi=0]=0.\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}(Y_{i}-Z_{i}^{\top}\vartheta_{\mathrm{cc}})\mid M_{i}=0]=0.

Their solution is unique under Assumption A3. Define

G^0=1ncc∑i:Mi=0ZiZi⊤,q^0=1ncc∑i:Mi=0ZiYi.\widehat{G}_{0}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i:M_{i}=0}Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top},\qquad\widehat{q}_{0}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i:M_{i}=0}Z_{i}Y_{i}.

The i.i.d. sampling specified in Subsection 3.1, positive complete-case probability, and finite moments in Assumption A3 imply, by the law of large numbers applied to selected sums and the complete-case fraction,

G^0→𝑝G0,q^0→𝑝G0​ϑcc.\widehat{G}_{0}\xrightarrow{p}G_{0},\qquad\widehat{q}_{0}\xrightarrow{p}G_{0}\vartheta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

Positive definiteness of G0G_{0} and the continuous mapping theorem give

ϑ^cc=G^0−1​q^0→𝑝ϑcc.\widehat{\vartheta}_{\mathrm{cc}}=\widehat{G}_{0}^{-1}\widehat{q}_{0}\xrightarrow{p}\vartheta_{\mathrm{cc}}.

In particular, β^cc→𝑝βcc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}}\xrightarrow{p}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}. The finite moments of h⁡(Xi)h(X_{i}) also give

1ncc∑i:Mi=0h(Xi)→𝑝𝔼[h(Xi)∣Mi=0].\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i:M_{i}=0}h(X_{i})\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb{E}[h(X_{i})\mid M_{i}=0].

Taking the inner product of this sample average with β^cc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}} therefore yields

τ^cc={1ncc∑i:Mi=0h(Xi)}⊤β^cc→𝑝𝔼[h(Xi)∣Mi=0]⊤βcc=τcc.\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}}=\left\{\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{cc}}}\sum_{i:M_{i}=0}h(X_{i})\right\}^{\top}\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb{E}[h(X_{i})\mid M_{i}=0]^{\top}\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

∎

Treatment-induced attrition

The complete-case ATE, τcc=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0]\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0], averages effects among units observed under the realized assignment. If treatment affects attrition, this group may differ under another assignment. In this case, Propositions 1–3 still hold. Under Corollary 3’s transport and support conditions, averaging complete-case conditional effects over the population covariate distribution recovers the population ATE.

D.4 Oracle specification and the indicator–error independence condition of Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018)

For the additive special case g⁡(Xi)=b⁡(Xi)g(X_{i})=b(X_{i}) and h⁡(Xi)=1h(X_{i})=1, the indicator–error independence condition of Arel-Bundock and Pelc (2018), written in our notation as Mi⟂εor,i|Di,XiM_{i}\perp\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i}, together with correct oracle specification, implies the zero conditional mean requirement in Proposition 2. Proposition 2 relaxes these specification and independence restrictions. Its additional graphical condition establishes the causal interpretation as the complete-case ATE, which is not addressed by their coefficient-preservation result.

Sufficient conditions

Suppose the oracle conditional mean is correctly specified:

Yi=βorDi+b(Xi)⊤γor+εor,i,𝔼[εor,i∣Di,Xi]=0.Y_{i}=\beta_{\mathrm{or}}D_{i}+b(X_{i})^{\top}\gamma_{\mathrm{or}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i}]=0.

Suppose also that

Mi⟂εor,i|Di,Xi,M_{i}\perp\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},

and Assumption A3 (complete-case OLS regularity) holds. Then the same regression among complete cases satisfies

𝔼[εcc,i∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=0.\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=0.

If {Xi,Mi}\{X_{i},M_{i}\} also satisfies the adjustment criterion and Assumptions A1 (SUTVA), A2 (complete-case treatment overlap), and A4 (complete-case population conditions) hold, then

τcc=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0],τ^cc→𝑝τcc.\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0],\qquad\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}}\xrightarrow{p}\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.
Proof.

Conditional independence and the correctly specified oracle conditional mean imply, on the complete-case support,

𝔼[εor,i∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=𝔼[εor,i∣Di,Xi]=0.\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i}]=0.

Consequently,

𝔼[Yi∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=βorDi+b(Xi)⊤γor.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=\beta_{\mathrm{or}}D_{i}+b(X_{i})^{\top}\gamma_{\mathrm{or}}.

These coefficients satisfy the complete-case population OLS normal equations. Assumption A3 ensures their uniqueness, giving βcc=βor\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\beta_{\mathrm{or}} and γcc=γor\gamma_{\mathrm{cc}}=\gamma_{\mathrm{or}}. Thus the complete-case residual εcc,i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i} equals εor,i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{or},i}, and

𝔼[εcc,i∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=0.\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cc},i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=0.

Under the adjustment criterion and Assumptions A1, A2, and A4, Proposition 2 therefore gives

τcc=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0],\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0],

and consistency of τ^cc\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}} under the maintained i.i.d. sampling in Subsection 3.1. ∎

These assumptions are stronger than the complete-case conditional mean condition in Proposition 2: the proof needs only preservation of the zero conditional residual mean, whereas conditional independence preserves the entire conditional outcome distribution given the regressors.

Violation of conditional independence in Mechanism B

Mechanism B violates this independence condition. Its oracle residual is Ui+ξiU_{i}+\xi_{i}, with 𝔼[Ui+ξi∣Di,Xi]=0\mathbb{E}[U_{i}+\xi_{i}\mid D_{i},X_{i}]=0. Because selection depends on UiU_{i}, however,

𝔼[Ui+ξi∣Di,Xi,Mi=0]=Xi2/2.\mathbb{E}[U_{i}+\xi_{i}\mid D_{i},X_{i},M_{i}=0]=X_{i}^{2}/2.

Thus the oracle residual is not conditionally independent of MiM_{i} given Di,XiD_{i},X_{i}, and the same intercept-and-linear-XiX_{i} specification no longer captures the complete-case mean. Nevertheless, the graphical adjustment condition still gives valid within-XiX_{i} treatment comparisons. Saturated outcome adjustment or treatment IPW can recover their common effect, as shown in the motivating simulation.

MAR does not generally imply the indicator–error independence condition: it permits selection on observed outcome values (Seaman et al. 2013). If only XiX_{i} can be missing while Yi,DiY_{i},D_{i} are observed, P⁡(Mi=0∣Yi,Di,Xi)=P⁡(Mi=0∣Yi,Di)P(M_{i}=0\mid Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i})=P(M_{i}=0\mid Y_{i},D_{i}) is MAR, yet selection through YiY_{i} may depend on the oracle residual. If only YiY_{i} can be missing and Di,XiD_{i},X_{i} are fully observed, MAR gives the indicator–error independence condition. With a correctly specified oracle conditional mean, it then preserves the zero conditional residual mean among complete cases.

D.6 Proof of Corollary 1

Under the conditions of Proposition 3, Proposition 1(i) gives Yi​(d)⟂Di|Xi,MiY_{i}(d)\perp D_{i}\mid X_{i},M_{i} for d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}, so the IPW identity in Proposition D.1 identifies the complete-case ATE. With e0​(x)=e¯0e_{0}(x)=\bar{e}_{0} constant, treatment is independent of XiX_{i} among complete cases, and P⁡(Di=1∣Mi=0)=𝔼⁡[e0​(Xi)∣Mi=0]=e¯0P(D_{i}=1\mid M_{i}=0)=\mathbb{E}[e_{0}(X_{i})\mid M_{i}=0]=\bar{e}_{0}. Thus, the distribution of XiX_{i} is the same in the treatment and control groups, and the IPW identity reduces to the difference between their average outcomes. For the treated term,

𝔼[Di​Yie¯0|Mi=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left.\frac{D_{i}Y_{i}}{\bar{e}_{0}}\right|M_{i}=0\right] =P⁡(Di=1∣Mi=0)e¯0𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Mi=0]\displaystyle=\frac{P(D_{i}=1\mid M_{i}=0)}{\bar{e}_{0}}\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,M_{i}=0]
=𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Mi=0].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,M_{i}=0].

Similarly, the untreated term equals 𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Mi=0]\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,M_{i}=0]. Hence,

𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Mi=0]=τcc.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,M_{i}=0]=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, βcc\beta_{\mathrm{cc}} is the coefficient from regressing YiY_{i} on the residual from projecting DiD_{i} on g⁡(Xi)g(X_{i}) among complete cases. Because 𝔼[Di∣Xi,Mi=0]=e¯0\mathbb{E}[D_{i}\mid X_{i},M_{i}=0]=\bar{e}_{0} and g⁡(Xi)g(X_{i}) includes an intercept, that residual is Di−e¯0D_{i}-\bar{e}_{0}. Let μd=𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Mi=0]\mu_{d}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,M_{i}=0] for d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\}. Since DiD_{i} is binary,

Cov⁡(Di,Yi∣Mi=0)\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}(D_{i},Y_{i}\mid M_{i}=0) =e¯0​μ1−e¯0​{e¯0​μ1+(1−e¯0)​μ0}\displaystyle=\bar{e}_{0}\mu_{1}-\bar{e}_{0}\{\bar{e}_{0}\mu_{1}+(1-\bar{e}_{0})\mu_{0}\}
=e¯0​(1−e¯0)​(μ1−μ0),\displaystyle=\bar{e}_{0}(1-\bar{e}_{0})(\mu_{1}-\mu_{0}),
Var⁡(Di∣Mi=0)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(D_{i}\mid M_{i}=0) =e¯0​(1−e¯0).\displaystyle=\bar{e}_{0}(1-\bar{e}_{0}).

Subtracting e¯0\bar{e}_{0} from DiD_{i} changes neither its covariance with YiY_{i} nor its variance. Thus,

βcc\displaystyle\beta_{\mathrm{cc}} =Cov⁡(Di−e¯0,Yi∣Mi=0)Var⁡(Di−e¯0∣Mi=0)\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(D_{i}-\bar{e}_{0},Y_{i}\mid M_{i}=0)}{\operatorname{Var}(D_{i}-\bar{e}_{0}\mid M_{i}=0)}
=𝔼[Yi∣Di=1,Mi=0]−𝔼[Yi∣Di=0,Mi=0]=τcc.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=1,M_{i}=0]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=0,M_{i}=0]=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}.

D.7 Proof of Corollary 2

Under a constant unit-level treatment effect, 𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=m]=τ\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=m]=\tau. Thus, by the law of total expectation,

𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)]=∫𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=m]​d​FM​(m)=∫τ​d​FM​(m)=τ.\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)]=\int\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=m]\,dF_{M}(m)=\int\tau\,dF_{M}(m)=\tau.

In particular, 𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Mi=0]=τ\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid M_{i}=0]=\tau. Substituting this equality into Proposition 2 gives τcc=τ\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau and consistency of τ^cc\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{cc}} under that proposition’s conditions. Proposition 3 gives β∗=τ\beta^{*}=\tau under its own conditions and consistency of β^\widehat{\beta} under Assumption A5 (estimated inverse-weight consistency). Corollary 1 gives βcc=τcc=τ\beta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}=\tau and consistency of β^cc\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cc}} under its own conditions.

D.8 Proof of Corollary 3

The complete-case support condition in Corollary 3, P⁡(Mi=0∣Wi=w)>0P(M_{i}=0\mid W_{i}=w)>0 for FpoWF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W}-almost every ww, ensures that τcc​(w)\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w) is defined throughout the population support of WiW_{i} up to a set of probability zero. By mean exchangeability given WiW_{i} and the law of iterated expectations,

∫τcc​(w)​d​FpoW​(w)\displaystyle\int\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w)\,dF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W}(w) =∫𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Wi=w]​d​FpoW​(w)\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid W_{i}=w]\,dF_{\mathrm{po}}^{W}(w)
=𝔼⁡[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)]=τ.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)]=\tau.

For the observed-outcome representation, Assumption A1 (SUTVA), Proposition 1(i) (conditional ignorability given the full adjustment vector), and Assumption A2 (complete-case treatment overlap) give, for d∈{0,1}d\in\{0,1\},

𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0] =𝔼[Yi(d)∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(d)\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]
=𝔼[Yi(d)∣Xi=x,Mi=0].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(d)\mid X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0].

Subtracting the expression for d=0d=0 from that for d=1d=1 gives δcc​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x). Since WiW_{i} is a subvector of XiX_{i}, iterated expectations within complete cases give

∫δcc​(x)​d​Fcc​(x∣Wi=w)\displaystyle\int\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\,dF_{\mathrm{cc}}(x\mid W_{i}=w) =𝔼[Yi(1)−Yi(0)∣Wi=w,Mi=0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid W_{i}=w,M_{i}=0]
=τcc​(w).\displaystyle=\tau_{\mathrm{cc}}(w).

This inner averaging uses only the covariate support among complete cases within each Wi=wW_{i}=w group. The transport and support assumptions at the WiW_{i} level then justify the outer population average. When Wi=XiW_{i}=X_{i}, the inner distribution is concentrated at x=wx=w, recovering the full-covariate result.

The following result applies Gabriel et al. (2024, Section 3 and Supporting Information S1) to complete cases.

Assumption A6 (Complete-case regression moments).

Proof of Proposition D.2

Let Zi=(1,Di,Xi⊤)⊤Z_{i}=(1,D_{i},X_{i}^{\top})^{\top} be the regressor vector and θ=(α,β,γ⊤)⊤\theta=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma^{\top})^{\top} be the coefficient vector.

Step 1: The population coefficients exist and are unique. Let ϕ⁡(Xi)\phi(X_{i}) be any function with 𝔼⁡[|ϕ⁡(Xi)|∣Mi=0]<∞\mathbb{E}[|\phi(X_{i})|\mid M_{i}=0]<\infty. Because 𝔼[Di∣Xi,Mi=0]=e0(Xi)\mathbb{E}[D_{i}\mid X_{i},M_{i}=0]=e_{0}(X_{i}), treatment overlap gives

Appendix E Simulation of the Collider–Mediator Dilemma

We assume the following data generation process, where the total causal effect of DD on YY is 0.8×1.5+0.8=20.8\times 1.5+0.8=2, while the controlled direct effect (Imai et al. 2011) of DD on YY is 0.80.8. The outcome YY is missing according to the latent index Li=1.5​Di+2​Ai+ηiL_{i}=1.5D_{i}+2A_{i}+\eta_{i}. The threshold cc in the missingness determination equation is selected such that the expected probability of missingness is 30%30\%, i.e. 𝔼⁡[Mi]=ℙ⁡(Li≥c)=0.3\mathbb{E}\left[M_{i}\right]=\mathbb{P}\left(L_{i}\geq c\right)=0.3.

Di\displaystyle D_{i} ∼B​e​r​n​o​u​l​l​i​(0.5)\displaystyle\sim Bernoulli\left(0.5\right)
Ai\displaystyle A_{i} =1+0.8​Di+ui,ui∼N⁡(0,1)\displaystyle=1+0.8D_{i}+u_{i},\qquad u_{i}\sim N\left(0,1\right)
Yi\displaystyle Y_{i} =1+0.8​Di+1.5​Ai+ζi,ζi∼N⁡(0,1)\displaystyle=1+0.8D_{i}+1.5A_{i}+\zeta_{i},\qquad\zeta_{i}\sim N\left(0,1\right)
Mi\displaystyle M_{i} =I{1.5Di+2Ai+ηi≥c},ηi∼N(0,1)\displaystyle=I\left\{1.5D_{i}+2A_{i}+\eta_{i}\geq c\right\},\qquad\eta_{i}\sim N\left(0,1\right)

We draw 10,000 samples of 5,000 observations. As in the main-text illustration, we estimate the oracle regression, complete-case regression with and without AiA_{i}, and multiple imputation. Here, the synthetic models use the variables in the DGP above, without additional baseline controls. For MI, we impute YY using (D,A)(D,A), or DD using (Y,A)(Y,A), and then regress YY on DD in the imputed datasets (Little and Rubin 2019).

Simulation Results

When YY is missing (Figure E2), neither complete-case regression estimates the total effect consistently: without AA, selection opens a noncausal path; controlling for AA blocks that path but also blocks the mediated effect. CCA+AA instead estimates the controlled direct effect, while MI recovers the total effect under the specified MAR mechanism. When DD is missing under the same index (Figure E2), neither complete-case regression nor MI recovers the total effect; missingness in DD depends on its own value.

Appendix F Reweighting for Generalized Linear Models

The distinction between conditional comparisons and their aggregation also applies to generalized linear models. Suppose the oracle conditional mean is

mpo(d,x):=𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x]=ℓ−1(α+βDd+x⊤γ).m_{\mathrm{po}}(d,x):=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x]=\ell^{-1}\!\left(\alpha+\beta_{D}d+x^{\top}\gamma\right).

For continuous DiD_{i}, the marginal effect is

apo​(d,x):=∂mpo​(d,x)∂d=βD​(ℓ−1)′​(α+βD​d+x⊤​γ).a_{\mathrm{po}}(d,x):=\frac{\partial m_{\mathrm{po}}(d,x)}{\partial d}=\beta_{D}\left(\ell^{-1}\right)^{\prime}\!\left(\alpha+\beta_{D}d+x^{\top}\gamma\right).

Although βD\beta_{D} is constant, the outcome-scale marginal effect generally varies with dd and xx. The oracle response function has a causal interpretation if XiX_{i} satisfies the adjustment criterion and SUTVA and treatment overlap hold.

Let mcc(d,x):=𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]m_{\mathrm{cc}}(d,x):=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0] and acc​(d,x):=∂mcc​(d,x)/∂da_{\mathrm{cc}}(d,x):=\partial m_{\mathrm{cc}}(d,x)/\partial d. With HccH_{\mathrm{cc}} and HpoH_{\mathrm{po}} denoting the complete-case and population distributions of (Di,Xi)(D_{i},X_{i}), the corresponding average marginal effects are

θcc=∫acc​(d,x)​d​Hcc​(d,x),θpo=∫apo​(d,x)​d​Hpo​(d,x).\theta_{\mathrm{cc}}=\int a_{\mathrm{cc}}(d,x)\,dH_{\mathrm{cc}}(d,x),\qquad\theta_{\mathrm{po}}=\int a_{\mathrm{po}}(d,x)\,dH_{\mathrm{po}}(d,x).

As in Subsection 5.1, recovering the population average requires both transport of the conditional effects and averaging over the population distribution. A sufficient condition for transporting the marginal-effect function is

𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x,Mi=0]=𝔼[Yi∣Di=d,Xi=x],\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x,M_{i}=0]=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}\mid D_{i}=d,X_{i}=x],

together with complete-case support; equality of the response functions implies equality of their derivatives where these exist. We can then fit a correctly specified GLM among complete cases and average its fitted marginal effects over HpoH_{\mathrm{po}}. If regressors are missing, their target distribution must be recovered, as discussed after Corollary 3. Consistent estimation of the GLM coefficients alone does not ensure consistent estimation of the population AME.

For binary treatment, use the probability contrast δcc​(x)=mcc​(1,x)−mcc​(0,x)\delta_{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=m_{\mathrm{cc}}(1,x)-m_{\mathrm{cc}}(0,x) in place of a derivative. Mean exchangeability of selection and treatment effect heterogeneity can transport this contrast without requiring equality of both response levels. Its population average then follows the same averaging argument as in Subsection 5.1.

Appendix G Estimates for the Reanalysis of Bodea and Hicks (2015)

Notes: CC means complete-case. The outcome is the signed log of inflation. All models include country fixed effects and the controls of Bodea and Hicks (2015): lagged log inflation, lagged money growth, lagged log GDP, lagged GDP growth, lagged trade openness, a de jure exchange-rate regime indicator, lagged fiscal balance, election indicators, and lagged world inflation. Panel A also includes Polity and reports coefficients and their difference per unit of CBI. The original-data estimate reproduces their Table 1, Model 5. The expanded data add country-years from countries covered by the updated CBI data, with controls rebuilt from public sources. The updated-CBI country target is labeled cbi144; the updated CBI data cover 143 countries and the European Central Bank. CC have every control observed. Panel B fits a separate regression for each moderator category and averages the category slopes using the CC shares, the shares among the updated-CBI countries (cbi144), or the shares across all countries Polity5 covers (worldwide), 1973–2008. Differences are the reweighted minus the CC average. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 country-cluster bootstrap draws, all draws succeeded. Target shares are held fixed in the bootstrap; CC shares are recomputed in each draw. Panel B reports raw and Holm-adjusted two-sided pp-values (raw/adjusted), with adjustment across the six moderators separately for each target; Panel A reports its unadjusted pp-value. Thinnest support is the smallest share, across a moderator's categories, of countries whose CBI changes within the category. The moderator categories are defined as follows: Polity, −10-10 to −6-6, −5-5 to 55, and 66 to 1010; executive constraints, 1–3, 4–6, and 7; political constraints, at most 0.2, above 0.2 through 0.4, and above 0.4; checks and balances, 1–2, 3, and 4 or more; Freedom House average rating, at most 2.5, above 2.5 through 5, and above 5; and press freedom, not free, partly free, and free.

Appendix H Treatment-IPW Comparison for the Canvassing Experiment

In another hypothetical example, had the researcher used a randomization scheme in which treatment probabilities differed by participants’ place of residence, assignment would depend on a component of XX, creating the arrow X→DX\rightarrow D. Suppose further that follow-up response depended on both XX and an unobserved determinant of the outcome, UU, as in Figure H1. Adjusting for XX would still preserve valid within-XX treatment comparisons, satisfying Box 1. However, selection could make the baseline outcome mean nonlinear in XX, as in mechanism B of the motivating simulation. A regression controlling only linearly for XX could then pool those comparisons incorrectly, so Box 2 would require an additional specification or weighting check.
